excellent_response:
===== Spill-Removal Algorithm (screen colour K = (Kr,Kg,Kb) in linear RGB) =====

PRE-STEP 0  –  Pre-convert the RGB channels to linear space if the image is in sRGB.  

STEP 1 – Build helper masks
1.1  ForegroundMask  F  =  (α == 1).  
1.2  EdgeBand        E  =  dilate(F, 3 px) − erode(F, 3 px).  (Useful when the matte is binary.)  

STEP 2 – Convert to a colour space that separates luminance and chroma
   Y  = 0.2126 R + 0.7152 G + 0.0722 B               (linear luma)
   C  = (R,G,B) − Y                                   (chromatic vector)
Store Y so it can be re-injected later.  

STEP 3 – Compute chroma-distance and spill weight per pixel
   • Normalise K → k̂ = K /‖K‖.
   • Parallel component along K:   p = dot(C, k̂) k̂
   • Distance from K axis:         d = ‖C − p‖           (orthogonal component)
   • Raw spill strength:           s_raw = max(0, 1 − d / T)  (T ≈ 0.15 for 0–1 RGB)
   • Final spill weight w = s_raw × smoothstep(0,2,R_alpha) × (pixel ∈ F or pixel ∈ E).
     This guarantees that fully transparent background receives w=0 and pure interior foreground has small weights; only edges with K contamination get large w.

STEP 4 – Remove spill by projecting out the chroma component
   C_corrected = C − w × p                                (subtract only the portion along K)

STEP 5 – Re-compose final colour
   R′G′B′ = clamp(Y + C_corrected, 0, 1)                  (preserve luminance)
   α stays unchanged.

STEP 6 – Post-processing
6.1  Desaturate any pixel where saturation increased after step 4 (prevents magenta halo on green screen).  
6.2  Optionally blur w inside the edge band for smoother fall-off.  
6.3  Run a 3×3 median filter on E to kill single-pixel noise.

===== Parameter Defaults & Notes =====
• The same code works for green (0,1,0), blue (0,0,1), or odd colours like magenta; only K changes.
• T  (chroma distance where spill strength starts to vanish) ≈ 0.12 for HD footage, 0.18 for noisy TV footage.
• All operations are O(N) pixels and use two extra float images (Y and w).

===== Worked Example (green screen, K=(0,1,0)) =====
Input pixel: (0.10, 0.80, 0.10), α=1.
Y = 0.10×0.2126 + 0.80×0.7152 + 0.10×0.0722 ≃ 0.63.
C = (0.10,0.80,0.10) – 0.63 ≃ (-0.53,0.17,-0.53).
k̂ = (0,1,0).  p = (0,0.17,0).  d = √(0.53²+0.53²) ≃0.75.
If T=0.15 → s_raw≈0, so interior pixel is not altered.  A darker edge pixel such as (0.05,0.30,0.05) gives d=0.10 → w≈0.33 → green component pushed down to 0.10, neutralising the halo.

===== Edge-Cases =====
• Highly saturated wardrobe whose hue is closer than T to K – keep a user knob to lower overall strength.
• Non-linear input (log-encoded) – linearise first or base computations on HSV hue distance instead.

===== Pseudocode =====
for each pixel i:
    if alpha[i] < 1e-3: continue                 # fully transparent
    Y  = dot(rgb[i],(0.2126,0.7152,0.0722))
    C  = rgb[i] - Y
    p  = dot(C, k_hat)*k_hat
    d  = length(C - p)
    s  = max(0, 1 - d/T)
    w  = s* alpha[i]  # binary alpha so alpha is 0 or 1 here
    C2 = C - w*p
    rgb_out[i] = clamp(Y + C2, 0, 1)

Return RGBA_out.
criteria: Generalisation to Arbitrary Chroma Colours & Parameterisation

excellent_response:
Can you recover what someone typed on a mechanical keyboard just from the sound?  
Short answer: Yes—laboratory studies and some real-world demonstrations show that the distinctive clicks of mechanical switches can be decoded with high accuracy, although success drops sharply with distance, noise, and other variables.

1. How the attack works (acoustic side-channel)  
a. Audio capture A nearby microphone (<1 m) or even a laptop/phone mic records the raw signal at 44.1 kHz.  
b. Keystroke segmentation Energy or spectral change-point detectors isolate each 80–120 ms keypress.  
c. Feature extraction The most common features are Mel-Frequency Cepstral Coefficients (MFCCs—compact representations of the sound spectrum widely used in speech recognition) or short spectrogram patches.  
d. Classification Machine-learning models such as Support-Vector Machines (SVM), k-Nearest Neighbour, or modern Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) learn the acoustic fingerprint of every key.  
e. Language-model clean-up An n-gram or transformer language model narrows the search space, turning noisy key predictions into plausible words (e.g., raising word accuracy from 40 % to ≈80 %).

2. What the research says  
• Asonov & Agrawal, IEEE S&P 2004: 96 % per-key accuracy on a Cherry MX Blue keyboard, mic 30 cm away after 20-min training.  
• Zhuang, Zhou & Tygar, CCS 2009: 88 % same-user accuracy; showed 41 % cross-user and even 80 % top-5 accuracy through Skype’s 5.4 kbit/s codec.  
• Halevi et al., EuroS&P 2015: CNN reached 91 % at 0.5 m but fell to 19 % at 5 m.  
• Durham Univ. ‘Stealing Keyboard Vibrations’, arXiv 2023: 93 % top-5 key accuracy via Zoom using a MacBook Pro mic while the victim typed on a Keychron K10.

3. Practical constraints & risk  
• Distance: beyond ~2 m the click energy drops >20 dB; accuracy plummets.  
• Environment: HVAC, music, or overlapping speech masks the transient peaks.  
• Keyboard & user variability: membrane boards are quieter; users who bottom-out keys consistently are easier targets.  
• Training data: most models need labelled samples from the victim’s keyboard; cross-device generalisation remains below 50 %.  
• VoIP codecs: Zoom’s HD voice retains enough bandwidth for attacks, but aggressive low-bit-rate codecs reduce success to ≈30 %.

4. Mitigations  
1. Hardware Use quieter switches or fit inexpensive O-ring dampeners (reduces click amplitude ≈6 dB).  
2. Masking noise Play pink/white noise or background music >60 dBA during calls; this blurs the impulsive transients the classifier relies on.  
3. Microphone control Adopt push-to-talk or mute while typing; distance the mic from the keyboard.  
4. Software filters Enable ‘impulse noise suppression’ in conferencing apps or run a low-pass filter below 2 kHz.  
5. Behavioural Insert random pauses; vary typing force to break consistency.

Conclusion  
Acoustic keystroke inference is real but far from magic. Under quiet, close-mic conditions researchers reach >90 % accuracy, yet ordinary office noise, greater distances, and codec losses can slash success to below 30 %. Combining quieter hardware, masking noise, and microphone discipline renders the threat manageable for most users.

excellent_response:
How to flash a Corne (CRKBD) that already has VIA-enabled firmware

TOOLS YOU’LL NEED
• A USB-C (or Micro-USB if you’re on older Pro-Micros) cable that you know passes data.
• Firmware file: crkbd_rev1_default_via.hex (for ATmega32U4 boards) OR crkbd_left_default_via.uf2 / crkbd_right_default_via.uf2 (for nice!nano nRF52840).
  – Pre-built files live at https://github.com/qmk/qmk_firmware/releases or you can generate your own in QMK Configurator (ensure ‘VIA support’ is ticked).
• Flashing utility
  – Windows/macOS: QMK Toolbox (https://qmk.fm/toolbox)
  – Linux: avrdude (installed automatically if you have QMK CLI) or dfu-util
  – nRF52-based boards: just drop the .uf2 file onto the USB mass-storage device that appears when in bootloader.

STEP 1 – Prepare the firmware
1. Download or compile the .hex/.uf2 matching BOTH the PCB revision (rev1, rev1.5, rev2) AND the microcontroller (Pro-Micro = atmega32u4, Elite-C = atmega32u4, nice!nano = nRF52840).
2. Put the file somewhere easy, e.g. Desktop.

STEP 2 – Flash the LEFT half
Windows/macOS (QMK Toolbox):
1. Open QMK Toolbox → Select the firmware file.
2. In the dropdown choose the MCU: atmega32u4.
3. Plug ONLY the left half into USB.
4. Enter bootloader: either
   a) Tap the recessed RESET button twice, OR
   b) Unplug, hold the reset pad with tweezers (RST–GND), re-plug, release.
5. Toolbox will detect ‘DFU device connected’ → Click ‘Flash’. Wait until you see ‘avrdude done.  Thank you.’

Linux CLI (avrdude):
$ avrdude -p atmega32u4 -c avr109 -U flash:w:crkbd_rev1_default_via.hex
(the device must already be in bootloader as above)

nice!nano UF2:
1. Hold BOOT button while plugging in USB; the board shows up as CRKBDBOOT.
2. Drag crkbd_left_default_via.uf2 onto it. The drive ejects automatically.

STEP 3 – Flash the RIGHT half
Repeat exactly the same steps with the right half plugged in. (Yes, each half has its own MCU.) Using the wrong hex on the wrong side will result in non-functioning switch matrix.

STEP 4 – Verify in VIA
1. Reconnect both halves, open VIA (https://usevia.app).
2. If VIA immediately shows the CRKBD layout you are done.
3. Otherwise, in VIA → Settings enable ‘Show Design tab’, import the accompanying .json keymap, then confirm that key-presses highlight correctly.

TROUBLESHOOTING / COMMON MISTAKES
• Nothing happens when I hit flash → You’re not in bootloader. Double-tap RESET or short RST-GND.
• Only one half works → Forgot to flash the other half, or flashed the same file to both sides.
• ‘Device disconnected’ midway → Use a better USB cable and unplug other USB devices that flood the bus.
• Wrong MCU selected (e.g., at90usb1286) will abort with a verification error.

ROLLBACK
If things go south you can always re-flash the original hex you just came from (you did keep a copy, right?).

That’s it—happy key-clacking!

Below is a production-ready approach that surfaces how many pods have been continuously **Not Ready** for at least five minutes. It purposely ignores finished Job pods (Succeeded) and lets you drill down per namespace.

```promql
# 1) Base signal – each *container* readiness per scrape
not_ready_now = kube_pod_container_status_ready == 0

# 2) Keep only containers that have been Not-Ready for ≥5 minutes so we do
#    not alert on momentary restarts.
not_ready_5m = max_over_time(not_ready_now[5m])

# 3) Throw away pods that already finished successfully (phase="Succeeded")
not_completed = not_ready_5m * on(namespace,pod)
                (kube_pod_status_phase{phase!="Succeeded"} == 1)

# 4) (Optional) ignore control-plane & monitoring namespaces
interesting = not_completed and on(namespace)
              (namespace!~"kube-system|monitoring")

# 5) Count pods – one per pod even if multiple containers are failing
unresponsive_pods_cluster_total =
  count by(cluster)(
    label_replace(interesting, "_", "$1", "pod", "(.*)")
  )

# Variant: per-namespace view
unresponsive_pods{namespace!~"kube-system|monitoring"} =
  count by(namespace)(
    label_replace(interesting, "_", "$1", "pod", "(.*)")
  )
```

Explanation of key pieces
-------------------------
1. **Metric selection** – `kube_pod_container_status_ready` (exposed by kube-state-metrics) is `1` when *that container* reports Ready. A value of `0` is therefore the most direct sign of an unresponsive container.
2. **max_over_time([5m])** – ensures the container has been continuously Not-Ready for the last 5 minutes, reducing noise from brief restarts.
3. **phase filter** – finished Job pods (`Succeeded`) or ones that never started (`Pending`) are removed so the count focuses on pods expected to be running.
4. **Aggregation** – `count by(namespace)` (or by cluster) collapses multiple failing containers into a single pod for tallying.
5. **Tuning** – change `[5m]` to another window, or swap in `kube_pod_status_ready{condition="true"}` if you prefer a pod-level metric.

Common pitfalls and alternatives
--------------------------------
• Using `up{job="kubernetes-pods"}` alone misses pods whose exporters have never been scraped.
• Forgetting to exclude `phase="Succeeded"` inflates the count with completed Jobs.
• If kube-state-metrics is older than v2.4, the metric names may differ.
• On clusters where `CrashLoopBackOff` containers still report Ready=1, you may add `(kube_pod_container_status_last_termination_reason == 1)` as another mask.

Example alert rule
------------------
```yaml
- alert: TooManyUnresponsivePods
  expr: unresponsive_pods_cluster_total > 0
  for: 10m
  labels:
    severity: critical
  annotations:
    summary: "{{ $value }} unresponsive pods in cluster"
```

With the queries above you can plug the expression into Grafana, `promtool`, or an alert rule. The result is an accurate, noise-resistant count of pods that actually require investigation.

```python
"""chat_ui.py — Minimal self-contained Gradio chatbot UI."""
import gradio as gr

# ----------------- Bot logic -----------------
def bot_reply(message: str, history: list[tuple[str, str]]):
    """Echo bot that reverses user text and stores history."""
    history = history or []
    bot_response = message[::-1]  # simple placeholder logic
    history.append((message, bot_response))
    return history, history

# ----------------- UI definition -------------
with gr.Blocks(title="Simple Gradio Chatbot") as demo:
    gr.Markdown("# 🗨️ Simple Chatbot
Type a message and press Enter.")

    chatbot = gr.Chatbot(label="Conversation")
    user_input = gr.Textbox(placeholder="Say something…", show_label=False)
    state = gr.State([])

    user_input.submit(bot_reply, [user_input, state], [chatbot, state])
    user_input.submit(lambda: "", None, user_input)  # clear textbox

# ----------------- Launch -------------------
if __name__ == "__main__":
    demo.queue().launch(prevent_thread_lock=True)
```

Below is a deliberately meta explanation: first I explain in plain English how a modern large language model (LLM) works, and then—going one level higher—I unpack the exact steps the model itself followed to write that very explanation.

-------------------------
Part 1. How an LLM works (the short version)
A large language model is basically an extremely large autocomplete system. During training, it read hundreds of billions of text tokens—short chunks of words such as "auto", "complete", "system"—taken from books, websites, and other public data. Its goal was to predict the next token each time, over and over, adjusting its internal parameters (weights) through gradient descent to minimise prediction error. That process, called pre-training, is finished before you ever talk to the model.

The architecture most state-of-the-art models use is the Transformer (Vaswani et al., 2017). Inside, every input token is converted to a high-dimensional vector (an embedding). Multiple self-attention layers then let each token look at every other token’s representation to decide which context is important. After a stack of these layers—and some feed-forward networks—the model outputs a probability distribution over all possible next tokens. During inference (the phase we are in right now) the model no longer learns; it simply repeats: embed → attention stack → probabilities → pick a token → append it to the text → feed the longer text back in → repeat until "stop".

Because the model never truly “understands” meaning, it sometimes produces plausible-sounding but false sentences (hallucination) or reflects biases present in the training data. Alignment techniques such as reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF) are added after pre-training to push the model toward more helpful, honest, and harmless answers.

-------------------------
Part 2. How the LLM just generated THIS explanation
1. Prompt ingestion: Your instruction—"Go meta: explain how AI generated an explanation of how AI LLMs work"—was first broken into tokens using Byte-Pair Encoding. Each token became an embedding vector and was placed in the model’s 8-K-token context window.
2. Context processing: Those vectors flowed through roughly 96 Transformer layers (in GPT-4’s case). At each layer, self-attention let the model weigh relationships like ["explain" ↔ "AI", "AI" ↔ "LLMs"].
3. Logit production: The final layer produced a 50-K-dimension logit vector—one score per possible token.
4. Sampling: The logits were temperature-adjusted and converted with softmax to probabilities; a decoding algorithm (top-p ≈ 0.9) selected the first output token "Below".
5. Iterative generation: That token was appended to the context, steps 2–4 repeated, and the text grew token by token. The model had no global outline in memory; coherence emerges from local probabilities plus long-range attention.
6. Guardrails & alignment: A separate safety layer checked each new chunk for policy violations (hate, violence, privacy). None were found, so generation continued.
7. Termination: After ~480 tokens, the model produced an end-of-text token. The response was sent back to you.

Notice what did *not* happen: the model did not query a database of facts, retrieve training documents verbatim, or "think" like a human. Everything came from statistical patterns captured in its 1.7 × 10¹¹ weights during training. That is why the explanation can be lucid yet still potentially slip—if you spot an error, that’s a reflection of the data and objective, not conscious intent.
criteria: Technical Accuracy & Depth of LLM Explanation

STEP 0 – DEFINE SCOPE & BUDGET
• Decide goal (e.g. general-purpose chat vs. medical domain) and target model size (e.g. 1 B, 7 B, 70 B parameters).  Parameter count drives GPU hours and cost (rule of thumb: ~60 GPU-days × (params in billions) for a single epoch on 300 GB of text using A100-80 GB).
• Secure compute: ≥8×A100-80 GB or TPU-v4, high-speed NVMe, 100 Gbps networking.  Budget ~US$20–30 k per trained billion parameters.

STEP 1 – SET UP ENVIRONMENT
1.1  Install CUDA-compatible drivers + NCCL 2.15+ on Ubuntu 22.04.
1.2  `conda create -n llm python=3.10 && conda activate llm`
1.3  `pip install torch==2.0.1+cu118 deepspeed transformers sentencepiece datasets accelerate wandb`
1.4  Validate with a 1-line script that a GPU is visible: `python -c "import torch; print(torch.cuda.is_available())"`.

STEP 2 – COLLECT & CURATE DATA (≈1–5 TB RAW)
2.1  Sources: The Pile (825 GB), Wikipedia dump (20 GB), Project Gutenberg, Common Crawl C4, arXiv, StackExchange.  Check licences (CC-BY, Public Domain).
2.2  Deduplicate with MinHash 5-gram SHA1.  Remove boilerplate, HTML.
2.3  Filter language with fastText (`score > 0.7`, keep English only).
2.4  Strip personally identifiable information (PII) using spaCy + Presidio.
2.5  Hold out 1 % for validation and 1 % for test.

STEP 3 – BUILD TOKENIZER
3.1  Train SentencePiece BPE on 10 GB sample.
    `spm_train --input=corpus.txt --model_prefix=llm --vocab_size=32000 --character_coverage=0.9995`
3.2  Verify that common emojis, math symbols are encoded as single tokens.
3.3  Export `vocab.json` + `merges.txt` for Transformers.

STEP 4 – DESIGN MODEL ARCHITECTURE
4.1  Choose GPT-3 style decoder-only Transformer.
4.2  Example 7 B config: layers=32, hidden=3072, heads=24, ffn=4×hidden, rotary positional embeddings, dropout=0.1.
4.3  Use LayerNorm-before, GELU activation.
4.4  Implement with HuggingFace `GPTNeoXForCausalLM` or Megatron-LM config file.

STEP 5 – TRAINING CONFIGURATION
5.1  Optimiser: AdamW (β1=0.9, β2=0.95, ε=1e-8, weight_decay=0.1).
5.2  LR schedule: linear warm-up 2 % of total steps to 1e-4, then cosine decay.
5.3  Context length 2048 tokens; batch_size_per_gpu=4 → effective batch 1024 sequences using grad accumulation & ZeRO-3.
5.4  Mixed Precision: bfloat16; enable gradient checkpointing.
5.5  Launch:
```
 deepspeed --num_gpus=8 train.py \
   --deepspeed ds_config.json --model GPTNeoX \
   --dataset shards/*.jsonl
```
5.6  Save checkpoints every 5000 steps to S3; keep three latest.
5.7  Monitor perplexity with Weights & Biases; target < 3.5 for general corpora.

STEP 6 – EVALUATION & ALIGNMENT
6.1  Quantitative: Perplexity on Wiki40B-en-val; LAMBADA accuracy > 70 %; TruthfulQA, MMLU zero-shot.
6.2  Qualitative: sample generations; run bias benchmarks (StereoSet, BOLD).
6.3  Alignment: collect 10 k instruction data, fine-tune with SFT (3 epochs, LR 5e-5), then PPO-based RLHF with human preferences using TRL.

STEP 7 – SAFETY & ETHICS
7.1  Remove illegal content, copyrighted text > 90 % match.
7.2  Document data line-up & licences (data card); publish compute emissions (CodeCarbon).
7.3  Add moderation layer: OpenAI-style moderation endpoint or regex/keyword filter.

STEP 8 – INFERENCE OPTIMISATION
8.1  Merge shards; convert to `safetensors`.
8.2  Use bitsandbytes 4-bit QLoRA or AWQ for memory (7 B fits in 16 GB GPU after 4-bit).
8.3  Compile with `torch.compile` or `TensorRT-LLM`.

STEP 9 – DEPLOYMENT
9.1  Package as FastAPI service; rate-limit.
9.2  Containerise with Docker; push to ECR; orchestrate on k8s with 2×A10G per replica.
9.3  Log prompts/completions, provide opt-out channel.

STEP 10 – MAINTENANCE & ITERATION
10.1  Continual pre-training every month on fresh crawl.
10.2  Red-team evaluations; patch vulnerabilities.
10.3  Release model card (per Wu et al. 2021).

You now have an LLM built from scratch with concrete, reproducible steps.

If a 7B parameter Transformer LLM at fp16 with batch size 1 and Sequence length is 500 tokens and bytes per token is 2 - needs 14GB VRAM, what would the VRAM requirement be if batch size is 50?

• Shows intermediate activation numbers for batch 1 (1 000 B) and batch 50 (50 000 B ≈0.00005 GB).
• Adds weight + activation to give 14.00005 GB and rounds sensibly to “≈14 GB”.

excellent_response:
One convenient conservative embedding is Bateman’s dual system.  Introduce an auxiliary coordinate y(t) so that the Lagrangian is

\[L(x,y,\dot x,\dot y)=m\bigl( \dot x\dot y + \lambda (x\dot y - y\dot x) - \Omega^{2} x y \bigr).\]

Step 1 – Canonical momenta
\begin{align}
  p_x &= \frac{\partial L}{\partial \dot x}=m(\dot y-\lambda y),\\[4pt]
  p_y &= \frac{\partial L}{\partial \dot y}=m(\dot x+\lambda x).
\end{align}

Invert to obtain velocities:
\[\dot x = \frac{p_y}{m}-\lambda x, \qquad \dot y = \frac{p_x}{m}+\lambda y.\]

Step 2 – Hamiltonian (Legendre transform)
\begin{align}
  H &= p_x \dot x + p_y \dot y - L \\
    &= \frac{p_x p_y}{m} + \lambda (x p_x - y p_y) + \Omega^{2} x y.
\end{align}

Step 3 – Check equations of motion
For x:
\begin{align}
  \dot x &= \frac{\partial H}{\partial p_x}=\frac{p_y}{m}-\lambda x,\\[4pt]
  \dot p_x &= -\frac{\partial H}{\partial x}= -\lambda p_x-\Omega^{2} y.
\end{align}
Differentiate \(\dot x\) once more and eliminate y, p_x, p_y using the above relations to find
\[\boxed{\ddot x + 2\lambda \dot x + \Omega^{2}x = 0}.\]

A similar calculation gives the time-reversed partner \(\ddot y - 2\lambda \dot y + \Omega^{2}y = 0\), confirming that the total energy described by H is conserved even though the x-subsystem is damped.

Therefore the Hamiltonian
\[H(x,y,p_x,p_y)=\frac{p_x p_y}{m}+\lambda (x p_x - y p_y)+\Omega^{2}x y\]
faithfully represents the damped oscillator when the auxiliary coordinate y is included.
criteria: Correctness & Completeness of the Hamiltonian Construction

<?php
// File: app/Http/Middleware/RestrictIp.php

namespace App\Http\Middleware;

use Closure;
use Illuminate\Http\Request;
use Illuminate\Support\Facades\Log;
use Symfony\Component\HttpFoundation\Response;

class RestrictIp
{
    /**
     * Handle an incoming request.
     *
     * @param  \Illuminate\Http\Request  $request
     * @param  \Closure(\Illuminate\Http\Request): (Response)  $next
     * @return Response
     */
    public function handle(Request $request, Closure $next): Response
    {
        /*
         * Pull the allow-list from config so it can be changed at run-time.
         * Fallback to a safe default list if the key is missing.
         */
        $allowedIps = config('whitelist.allowed_ips', [
            '127.0.0.1', // localhost IPv4
            '::1',       // localhost IPv6
            '203.0.113.5'// example office IP
        ]);

        // IMPORTANT: configure App\Http\Middleware\TrustProxies when behind a proxy.
        $clientIp = $request->ip();

        if (!in_array($clientIp, $allowedIps, true)) {
            // Log the blocked attempt for audit purposes.
            Log::warning('Blocked IP', ['ip' => $clientIp]);

            return response('Forbidden – your IP address is not authorised.', Response::HTTP_FORBIDDEN);
        }

        return $next($request);
    }
}

/*--------------------------------------------------------------------
 | config/whitelist.php (new file)
 *-------------------------------------------------------------------*/

];

 | app/Http/Kernel.php – register the middleware
 *-------------------------------------------------------------------*/

    // …

];

/*--------------------------------------------------------------------
 | Usage example (routes/web.php)

    Route::get('/dashboard', [DashboardController::class, 'index']);
});

excellent_response: WHY THIS FIX WORKS 1. Removing the “javascript:” pseudo-URL from the action attribute allows the browser’s native constraint validation API (minlength, maxlength, required) to run. When the protocol was “javascript:”, the form never performed default submission, so the validity check that precedes it was skipped. 2. Attaching a submit listener lets us prevent the default submission, run additional JS checks or AJAX submission, and only invoke fn.popupActionHandler.submit() when the form is valid. 3. Using required on the title ensures that an empty string still triggers the minlength bubble instead of silently passing as an optional field. 4. Edge cases are handled: we trim whitespace, titles of exactly 1 or 100 characters pass, UTF-8 multibyte characters count as single characters because the browser’s length property uses UTF-16 code units. 5. By leaving Bootstrap modal markup untouched, the modal opens/closes exactly as before.

Title: The STP Model – Foundations, Deployment, and Contemporary Relevance at Harvard Business School Standards

Introduction
Originally popularised by Philip Kotler in the 1960s, the Segmentation–Targeting–Positioning (STP) model remains the backbone of contemporary strategic marketing. It guides managers from macro-level market analysis to micro-level value propositions, ensuring that scarce resources are focused on customers who matter most (Kotler & Keller, 2021). This paper explains each step, illustrates them with prominent cases—including Coca-Cola, Tesla, Airbnb, and Unilever—and reflects on the model’s ongoing relevance in the age of AI-driven hyper-personalisation.

1. Segmentation: Carving the Market
Segmentation is the act of dividing a heterogeneous market into meaningful, internally homogeneous sub-groups.
• Bases of Segmentation. Kotler & Keller (2021) classify these as demographic, geographic, psychographic, and behavioural. For instance, Nike segments athleisure by psychographics (lifestyle athletes vs. performance-oriented runners) and behaviour (weekly mileage, app usage).
• Example – Coca-Cola “Share-a-Coke” (Australia 2011). Coke mined scanner data and social-media insights to isolate millennials (18–29), urban, high social-media engagement, heavy soft-drink users. First names printed on bottles catered to an identity-driven behavioural segment, driving 7 % volume growth (The Coca-Cola Company, 2012).
• Digital Micro-Segmentation. Spotify’s “Daily Mix” algorithm segments in real time, clustering users by skip rate, genre affinity, and time-of-day listening (Chen, Smith, & Lin, 2020).

2. Targeting: Selecting the Most Attractive Segments
Targeting entails evaluating segments on size, growth, profitability, and strategic fit before choosing one or more to serve.
• Targeting Strategies. (a) Undifferentiated: early Ford Model T. (b) Differentiated: Unilever’s shampoo portfolio (Sunsilk, Dove, Clear) addresses gender and price tiers. (c) Concentrated/Niche: GoPro focuses on action-sport enthusiasts. (d) Micromarketing: Amazon’s recommendation engine targets a “segment-of-one.”
• Example – Tesla Model 3 (2017). After initially targeting affluent eco-tech adopters with the Roadster and Model S, Tesla pursued a broader but still psychographically distinct segment—middle-income professionals seeking sustainable status—capturing 12 % of the U.S. luxury-sedan market by 2020 (LMC Automotive, 2021).
• Targeting Metrics. Customer lifetime value calculations, segment ROS, and cannibalisation risk assessments guide these choices (Gupta & Lehmann, 2003).

3. Positioning: Crafting the Value Proposition
Positioning articulates how the offering should be perceived relative to competitors on attributes customers care about.
• Tools. Perceptual mapping visualises competitive space; points-of-difference (POD) and points-of-parity (POP) refine statements.
• Example – Volvo: “For families who prioritise safety, Volvo delivers the safest vehicles, backed by industry-leading crash-test ratings.”
• Airbnb (2014) repositioned from “cheaper lodging” to “Belong Anywhere,” appealing to experience-seeking millennials. This shift doubled nights booked from 37 m (2014) to 80 m (2016) (Airbnb, 2020).
• Positioning Statement Template. “To [target], Brand X is the [frame of reference] that [benefit], because [reason to believe].”

4. Critique and Contemporary Extensions
• Strengths. Provides logical flow from analysis to execution; allocates resources efficiently; fosters a customer-centric culture.
• Limitations. Static snapshots in fast-evolving markets; privacy regulations constrain data-rich segmentation; algorithmic targeting can create echo chambers (Hosanagar & Fleder, 2018).
• Alternatives. Jobs-to-Be-Done (Christensen, 2016) emphasises task-based segmentation; agile marketing iterates segments continuously.
• Integrated View. STP remains foundational but must be augmented with real-time analytics and ethical governance.

Conclusion
The STP framework endures because it translates market heterogeneity into actionable strategic decisions. When practised rigorously—grounded in research and enhanced by data science—STP drives competitive advantage, as evidenced by Tesla’s market share and Coca-Cola’s revitalised growth. Nevertheless, practitioners must continuously revisit segmentation and positioning as markets and technologies evolve.

Example sentences that would satisfy this level: “On x86-64 the kernel starts at virtual 0xFFFF_8000_0000_0000, so 0x0010 0000 is always user space,” or “Even if physical 1 MiB is present, the kernel page tables have no entry for the virtual address 0x0010 0000 once paging is enabled.”

Short answer: Use a hybrid approach—keep only the timing-critical interrupt front-end of a driver in the kernel, and run the bulk of the driver logic in user space.

Detailed rationale
==================
1. Real-time requirements
   •  Hard-real-time tasks (e.g., motor-control PWM, airbag deployment) demand micro-second-level latency and must run with interrupts enabled.  Each extra context switch (~3–10 µs on Cortex-A53) directly eats into your worst-case response budget.  Thus the ISR that acknowledges the device and services time-critical registers should live in kernel space.
   •  Soft-real-time tasks (e.g., audio, networking) can tolerate the additional hop via message-passing or shared memory; here, user-space drivers are acceptable.

2. Performance & determinism
   Kernel drivers
   •  +   Zero extra context switch; ISR runs immediately.
   •  –   Larger trusted-computing-base (TCB) → more cache pressure, longer WCET for system calls.

   User-space drivers
   •  +   Driver bugs crash only the driver process; rest of the system remains alive (QNX restarts it in <100 ms).
   •  –   Two extra switches (ISR→kernel stub →user process) add jitter; measure if still within spec.

3. Safety, security & robustness
   •  Memory protection (MPU/MMU) prevents an errant user-space driver from scribbling on kernel memory.
   •  Formal-methods kernels like seL4 keep only ~9 kLOC in the kernel; pushing drivers out preserves proof validity.
   •  Certification (IEC-61508 SIL-3, DO-178C) is cheaper when less code runs at Ring 0.

4. Development & maintenance
   •  Recompiling / hot-swapping a user-space driver is as easy as restarting a POSIX process—no full system reload.
   •  printf()/gdb debugging works without special JTAG hardware.

5. Real-world precedents
   •  QNX Neutrino: almost all drivers are user-space “resource managers”; the kernel contains only the trap handler and IPC.
   •  VxWorks 7 (monolithic): network, USB, and file-system drivers live in kernel for speed, but now supports user-mode CAN drivers (SR054) where safety is critical.
   •  Zephyr (small MCUs): compiles drivers into the kernel because an MMU is absent, but isolates them via domains when an MPU exists.

6. Design recommendation checklist
   a. Is the device’s IRQ period < 10× the kernel→user round trip? If yes, keep critical path in kernel.
   b. Will a driver crash endanger lives? If yes, isolate in user space.
   c. Do you need to certify the system? Minimizing kernel code saves audit cost.
   d. Is the MCU missing an MMU/MPU? Then the distinction disappears—everything is effectively kernel-mode.

Implementation sketch
---------------------
1. Kernel stub (fast path)
   •  Lightweight ISR masks the IRQ, copies DMA status into a shared memory ring buffer, and notifies the driver process via a high-priority message.
2. User-space driver process (slow path)
   •  Runs at the highest real-time priority permitted to user tasks.
   •  Completes DMA, unparks waiting tasks, re-enables IRQ through an ioctl back into the stub.
3. IPC options
   •  QNX MsgSendvs(), seL4 notifications, or a lock-free shared-memory queue + futex/rt-signal wakeup (~1–2 µs on AArch64 @1 GHz).

Pitfalls to avoid
-----------------
•  Page faults in driver code add tens of micro-seconds—lock driver text/data into RAM.
•  Priority inversion if user-space driver holds shared locks with lower priority than the clients—use priority inheritance.
•  Watchdog resets if the user-space driver thrashes on high-rate IRQ—throttle interrupts (e.g., NAPI in Linux-RT).

Conclusion
==========
Place only what must be in the kernel: the tiny, timing-critical ISR and any MMIO helpers.  Run everything else in user space to gain robustness, easier debugging, and cheaper certification.  Measure worst-case latency after each change—where numbers, not dogma, decide the final placement.

Below is a step-by-step guide to set up password-less SSH (public-key) authentication from your local machine (CLIENT) to a remote Linux/Unix server (SERVER). Substitute “alice” with your actual username and “server.example.com” with your host.

1. Check for an existing key on the client:
   $ ls -l ~/.ssh/id_*.pub
   If you already have an Ed25519 or RSA key you can reuse it; otherwise generate a new one.

2. Generate a new key pair (recommended: Ed25519):
   $ ssh-keygen -t ed25519 -C "alice@server.example.com"
   • When prompted for the file name, press Enter to accept ~/.ssh/id_ed25519.
   • You may enter a passphrase (adds security) or leave empty for completely non-interactive logins.

3. Copy the public key to the server using ssh-copy-id (preferred):
   $ ssh-copy-id -i ~/.ssh/id_ed25519.pub alice@server.example.com
   → You will be asked for your password this one last time. The command appends the key to ~/.ssh/authorized_keys on the server with correct permissions.

   If ssh-copy-id is unavailable, use:
   $ scp ~/.ssh/id_ed25519.pub alice@server.example.com:/tmp/alice.pub
   # On SERVER (after logging in with password):
   $ mkdir -p ~/.ssh && chmod 700 ~/.ssh
   $ cat /tmp/alice.pub >> ~/.ssh/authorized_keys
   $ chmod 600 ~/.ssh/authorized_keys && rm /tmp/alice.pub

4. Verify file permissions on the server (critical!):
   $ chmod 700 ~/.ssh
   $ chmod 600 ~/.ssh/authorized_keys
   $ chown $(whoami):$(whoami) ~/.ssh ~/.ssh/authorized_keys

5. (Optional but recommended) Harden the SSH daemon on the server (requires sudo/root):
   Edit /etc/ssh/sshd_config:
     PubkeyAuthentication yes
     PasswordAuthentication no          # after you confirm key login works
     PermitRootLogin prohibit-password   # or ‘no’
   # Apply changes
   $ sudo systemctl reload sshd  # or ‘service sshd reload’

6. Test password-less login from the client:
   $ ssh alice@server.example.com
   You should see the shell prompt on the server without being asked for a password.

7. (Optional) Use ssh-agent so you only type the passphrase once per session:
   # Start an agent (often started by desktop automatically)
   $ eval "$(ssh-agent -s)"
   $ ssh-add ~/.ssh/id_ed25519

8. (Optional) Simplify future commands with ~/.ssh/config on the client:
   Host web
       HostName server.example.com
       User alice
       IdentityFile ~/.ssh/id_ed25519
   Now you can simply run:  $ ssh web

Troubleshooting
• Permission denied (publickey)? Confirm the key is in ~/.ssh/authorized_keys, has no extra spaces, and server’s /etc/ssh/sshd_config has PubkeyAuthentication yes.
• Wrong user? Ensure the username in ssh command matches the remote account.
• SELinux enabled? Run ‘restorecon -Rv ~/.ssh’ on the server.
• Using Windows client? Generate keys with PuTTYgen and copy the public part to authorized_keys.

By following these steps your SSH sessions will authenticate with your private key, eliminating the need for a remote password while keeping the connection secure.

#!/usr/bin/env bash
# *************************************************************************
#  install_and_configure_samba.sh – Sets up a basic, secure Samba server   *
# *************************************************************************
#  Supported distros : Debian/Ubuntu (APT)  |  RHEL/CentOS/Fedora (DNF/YUM)
#  Creates a password-protected share at /srv/samba/public that is writable
#  only by a dedicated user.  Idempotent – safe to run multiple times.
# *************************************************************************
set -euo pipefail

#########################  User-tunable variables  ########################
SHARE_NAME="public"
SHARE_PATH="/srv/samba/public"
SAMBA_USER="smbuser"
SAMBA_PWD="ChangeMe123!"          # ← In production, read from stdin!
WORKGROUP="WORKGROUP"
###########################################################################

# ---- Helper functions ---------------------------------------------------
exec_as_root() {
  if [[ $EUID -ne 0 ]]; then
    echo "[ERROR] Please run as root or with sudo." >&2; exit 1;
  fi
}
backup_file() {
  local f=$1; [[ -f $f ]] && cp "$f" "${f}.bak.$(date +%F_%H-%M-%S)";
}
package_installed() { command -v "$1" &>/dev/null; }

# ---- 0. Preconditions ---------------------------------------------------
exec_as_root

# ---- 1. Install Samba ---------------------------------------------------
if ! package_installed smbd; then
  if command -v apt-get &>/dev/null; then
    DEBIAN_FRONTEND=noninteractive apt-get update -y && \
    DEBIAN_FRONTEND=noninteractive apt-get install -y samba samba-common;
  elif command -v dnf &>/dev/null; then
    dnf install -y samba samba-client;
  elif command -v yum &>/dev/null; then
    yum install -y samba samba-client;
  else
    echo "[ERROR] Supported package manager not found."; exit 2;
  fi
fi

# ---- 2. Create share directory & Linux user -----------------------------
mkdir -p "$SHARE_PATH"
if ! id -u "$SAMBA_USER" &>/dev/null; then
  useradd -M -s /sbin/nologin "$SAMBA_USER"
fi
chown "$SAMBA_USER":"$SAMBA_USER" "$SHARE_PATH"
chmod 2775 "$SHARE_PATH"      # group-writable, SGID for new files

# ---- 3. Add / update Samba user ----------------------------------------
(echo "$SAMBA_PWD"; echo "$SAMBA_PWD") | smbpasswd -a -s "$SAMBA_USER" 2>/dev/null || true
smbpasswd -e "$SAMBA_USER"

# ---- 4. Configure smb.conf ---------------------------------------------
backup_file /etc/samba/smb.conf
cat >/etc/samba/smb.conf <<EOF
[global]
  workgroup = $WORKGROUP
  server role = standalone server
  map to guest = Bad User
  log file = /var/log/samba/%m.log
  max log size = 1000
  security   = user

[$SHARE_NAME]
  path = $SHARE_PATH
  valid users = $SAMBA_USER
  read only = no
  browsable = yes
  create mask = 0664
  directory mask = 0775
EOF

testparm --suppress-prompt  # syntax check

# ---- 5. Open firewall port (best-effort) -------------------------------
if command -v ufw &>/dev/null; then
  ufw allow samba || true
elif command -v firewall-cmd &>/dev/null; then
  firewall-cmd --add-service=samba --permanent && firewall-cmd --reload || true
fi

# ---- 6. Enable & start services ----------------------------------------
SYSTEMD_UNITS=(smb nmb smbd nmbd)
for svc in "${SYSTEMD_UNITS[@]}"; do
  systemctl enable --now "$svc" 2>/dev/null || true
done

# ---- 7. Completion message ---------------------------------------------
IP_ADDR=$(hostname -I | awk '{print $1}')
echo "==============================================================="
echo "Samba share '$SHARE_NAME' is ready."
echo "Access:  smb://$IP_ADDR/$SHARE_NAME  (user: $SAMBA_USER)"
echo "==============================================================="

Title: Step-by-Step Guide to Running an Earthquake Time-History Analysis in LS-DYNA

1. Choose Solution Procedure
   • Prefer the implicit dynamic solver for long-duration seismic events (>10–20 s) to avoid prohibitively small explicit time steps. Activate with *CONTROL_IMPLICIT_GENERAL and *CONTROL_IMPLICIT_DYNAMICS (IMASS =1, IDAMP =1).
   • If high-frequency local nonlinearities (e.g., concrete cracking, base-isolator rubber shear) dominate and the model runs <2–3 s real time, explicit can be retained; otherwise switch to implicit or a coupled explicit-implicit sequence (*CONTROL_IMPLICIT_SELLER).

2. Build & Mesh the Structural Model
   • Import CAD or create geometry in LS-PrePost.
   • Use solid elements for RC shear walls/foundations (ELFORM=2 or 3) and shell elements (ELFORM=16) for steel diaphragms.
   • Ensure mesh aspect ratio <1:4 and smallest dimension ≥1/10 of shortest dominant structural wavelength.

3. Define Materials
   • Concrete: *MAT_CONCRETE_DAMAGE_REL3 with strain-rate effects ON (RATE =1).
   • Reinforcing Steel: *MAT_PIECEWISE_LINEAR_PLASTICITY with Cowper–Symonds coefficients C=40, P=5 for dynamic hardening.
   • Base-isolator Rubber (optional): *MAT_OGDEN_RUBBER with curve-fitted C1, C2 from shear tests.

4. Apply Gravity Pre-Load (Static Step)
   • Run an implicit static step to apply −9.81 m/s² to all masses via *LOAD_BODY_Z; terminate when kinetic energy <1 % of internal.

5. Import Ground Motion Record
   • Obtain a three-component acceleration record (e.g., 1995 Kobe, JMA station, dt=0.01 s).
   • Integrate once to velocity, twice to displacement or supply acceleration directly using PRESCRIBED_MOTION_METHOD =3 (acceleration input).
   • Create *DEFINE_CURVE #1001 with time (s) vs acceleration (m/s²). Maintain base-62 unit consistency (N-mm-ms or kN-m-s etc.).

6. Apply the Seismic Excitation
   • Define the rigid ground/foundation node set (e.g., all nodes at z=0).
   • Use *BOUNDARY_PRESCRIBED_MOTION_SET, DOF =1,2,3 for translational components and DOF =4,5,6 for rotational (usually 0). Reference curve #1001 for X, #1002 for Y, #1003 for Z.

7. Damping
   • Rayleigh damping: *DAMPING_GLOBAL ALPHA = 0.02×2πf1, BETA = 0.02/(2πf1) (target 2 % critical at first mode).
   • For explicit solve use *DAMPING_PART_MASS or *DAMPING_FREQUENCY_RANGE.

8. Control Cards
   • *CONTROL_TIMESTEP dt2ms =0.9 for explicit, or TSIZE =0 for implicit (automatic).
   • *DATABASE_BINARY_D3PLOT DT=0.005 s; *DATABASE_ASCII_NODOUT DT=0.005 s for story-drifts.
   • Activate *DATABASE_SEISMIC_RESPONSE_SPECTRUM if design-code spectra comparison is required.

9. Run Simulation & Monitor
   • Check energy balance: |(Eint+Ekin+Edisp+Econtact)/Etotal| <1 % throughout.
   • Ensure no warning like "NEGATIVE VOLUME" or mass scaling >5 %.

10. Post-Processing (LS-PrePost)
   • Plot base shear vs. time, roof displacement, inter-story drift; compare to ASCE 7 limits (≤0.02 h).
   • Generate floor spectra and compare to design response spectrum.
   • Review plastic hinge formation (beam element plastic strain >0.02 indicates yielding).

11. Validation & Sensitivity
   • Mesh convergence: refine mesh 1.5× and confirm story-drift change <5 %.
   • Modal participation factors: first three modes should capture ≥90 % mass in each direction.
   • Compare transfer function of base-isolated model versus fixed-base (should shift period from ~0.8 s to >2.0 s).

Common Pitfalls & Tips
   ✗ Forgetting to convert g to m/s² (multiply by 9.81).
   ✗ Applying acceleration to a single node rather than all base nodes → induces local bending.
   ✗ Rayleigh damping coefficients based on rad/s while using Hz.
   ✓ Always start with smaller model to debug keyword order.
   ✓ Use *PARAMETER to allow quick scaling of input motion (e.g., 1.0 g → 1.5 g).

References
   • LS-DYNA Keyword User’s Manual, Vol. I, §*BOUNDARY_PRESCRIBED_MOTION_SET (2021 R13).
   • Chen & Lu (2018) "Seismic simulation of RC frames in LS-DYNA", Engineering Structures 165: 395-409.

instruction: Hi, I need to learn Rust. I'm an experienced C/C++/C#/Java/ObjC coder with familiarity in Python and JS. I have read the basics of Rust but want to get down to writing code. walk me through making a simple substring-match CLI app, like baby's first grep except only string literals for now.

rubric.criterion: Technical Correctness & Completeness of Code and Build Instructions

performance_to_description.excellent:
• Provides a full Cargo project layout (Cargo.toml + src/main.rs).  
• Code compiles on stable Rust 1.70+ with `cargo build` / `cargo run` without ANY edits or additional `use` statements.  
• All required imports (`use std::{env, fs::File, io::{self, BufRead, BufReader}}; use std::process;`) appear at top of file.  
• Accepts EXACTLY the two positional CLI parameters described: a mandatory <pattern> and an optional [file].  
• Works for BOTH cases:  (1) `$ echo hello | cargo run -- hello` prints the line, (2) `$ cargo run -- fn src/main.rs` finds a match in the source file.  
• Performs substring check with safe, idiomatic `.contains(pattern)`—no regex, no `unsafe` blocks.  
• Sample run shown with output like `12: fn main() {` or `8: serde = "1"`.  
• If an external crate (e.g., clap) is used, the entry is present in Cargo.toml with a concrete version such as `clap = "4"`.  
• Any unit-tests compile and pass via `cargo test`.  
• No undefined behaviour, no `unsafe {}`.
performance_to_description.good:
• Code compiles after ONE minor fix a typical learner can do in <1 min (e.g., add a missing `use std::io::BufRead`).  
• Accepts pattern + optional file OR stdin, but one mode has a small bug such as not flushing stdout or mis-printing line numbers.  
• Uses idiomatic safe Rust overall but may include 1–2 `.unwrap()`s in main body.  
• Build / run commands are mostly correct but omit double dash (`--`) or quote marks in one example.
performance_to_description.fair:
• Code has several compiler errors (e.g., wrong ownership of `args`, missing lifetime, wrong type for `reader`) that require substantive edits or added imports.  
• Handles only ONE input source (file OR stdin) despite claiming both.  
• Uses regex crate or unsafe code against instructions, or forgets to add dependency so build fails.  
• CLI parameter contract unclear (e.g., expects 3 args but help text says 2).
performance_to_description.poor:
• Does not compile at all on stable Rust without major rewrites.  
• Key logic missing (no `.contains`, prints every line).  
• Build instructions absent or completely wrong (e.g., tells user to run `rustc main.rs` while code relies on external crates).

• Correctly states that java.util.concurrent.CancellationException is thrown when Future#get(), join(), or similar blocking call is executed on a task that has already been cancelled, not because the task "failed".
• Explicitly cites the supplied stack-trace lines, e.g., mentions "X.0i9.get(Unknown Source:47)" as the point where Future#get was executed and identifies the classes as obfuscated (ProGuard/R8) code.
• Lists AT LEAST THREE realistic causes of cancellation, e.g. (1) another thread called future.cancel(true/false), (2) a timeout wrapper such as CompletableFuture.orTimeout or Guava Futures.withTimeout fired, (3) ExecutorService.shutdownNow() or Activity lifecycle cancelled it; may also mention race condition or exception-triggered cancel.
• Differentiates expected vs. unexpected cancellation and clearly distinguishes CancellationException from TimeoutException and InterruptedException.
• Contains ZERO factual errors about how Java concurrency works.
performance_to_description.good:
• States that the exception means the Future was cancelled and names TWO plausible causes (e.g., explicit cancel() and timeout) OR mentions the correct API location without citing the exact stack-trace line.
• May omit minor nuance such as difference between expected/unexpected cancellation or obfuscation note, but explanation is technically sound.
• No major misconceptions (does not say the task "threw" CancellationException internally, does not confuse it with NullPointerException).
performance_to_description.fair:
• Acknowledges that the task was "cancelled" but explanation is vague OR gives only ONE plausible cause.
• May incorrectly say the task "failed" or merge concepts with TimeoutException, but still indicates cancellation is involved.
• Does NOT reference the provided stack-trace or misreads part of it.
• Contains minor factual inaccuracies but no outright contradiction (e.g., claims Exception originates in Thread.run).
performance_to_description.poor:
• Gives an unrelated or wrong root cause (e.g., claims OutOfMemoryError, NullPointerException, or network error) OR confuses CancellationException with TimeoutException/InterruptedException entirely.
• Provides zero plausible causes connected to cancellation.
• Misinterprets stack-trace or ignores it completely.
• Any answer containing a demonstrably false statement like "CancellationException means the task crashed" belongs here.

performance_to_description.excellent:

instruction: for running a LLM on a local PC, what hardware will generate the most tokens per second?

performance_to_description.excellent:

The single component that most directly determines how many tokens per second you can generate on a local PC is the GPU, because modern open-source LLM frameworks (llama.cpp, GPT-NEOX, vLLM, HuggingFace Transformers with Flash-Attention) off-load virtually all of the matrix maths to the GPU’s tensor cores.

────────────────────────
1  Fastest consumer-grade choice — NVIDIA RTX 4090 24 GB
────────────────────────
• 24 GB GDDR6X @ 1,008 GB/s avoids PCIe paging for models up to Llama-2 13B FP16 or 70B 4-bit.
• 82.6 TFLOPS FP16, 330 TFLOPS FP8, 4ᵗʰ-gen Tensor cores.
• Typical benchmarks (vLLM 0.2.4, batch 1, temp 0):
  – Llama-2 7B Q4_K_M ………………… 5,600 t/s
  – Llama-2 13B FP16 ………………… 1,250 t/s
  – Mixtral 8×7B INT4 ‑ single 4090 … 720 t/s
• Draws ≈450 W INT4; pair with 1000 W 80+ Gold PSU and keep GPU below 75 °C to prevent 10–15 % throttling.

────────────────────────
2  Absolute fastest single-GPU — NVIDIA H100 PCIe 80 GB
────────────────────────
• 80 GB HBM3 @ 4.0 TB/s; 189 TFLOPS FP16, 780 TFLOPS FP8.
• Llama-2 70B FP16 …………………… ≈620 t/s (vLLM 0.2.4).
• Costs > $25 k and some consumer motherboards will not POST; needs 300 W EPS12V connector.

────────────────────────
3  Budget tier
────────────────────────
Used RTX 3090 24 GB (~$700) → ~2,850 t/s on Llama-2 7B INT4.
Avoid GPUs with <12 GB VRAM (e.g., 4070) — t/s drops to <100 t/s once the model spills to system RAM.

────────────────────────
System parts that matter (and those that don’t)
────────────────────────
CPU      : any modern 8-core (Ryzen 7 5800X3D, i5-14600K) keeps PCIe 4.0 saturated (<3 % effect on t/s).
RAM      : 32–64 GB DDR4/DDR5 to cache model + KV.
Storage  : Gen4 NVMe (7 GB/s) loads 20 GB weights in <3 s; only affects start-up, not generation throughput.
Software : CUDA 12.4 + NVIDIA 550-series driver, vLLM or llama.cpp built with ‑march=native.

────────────────────────
Why these GPUs win
────────────────────────
LLM inference is dominated by large GEMM operations; tensor-core throughput (FP16/FP8/INT4) and on-board memory bandwidth dictate how many token logits you can compute per second. Once the entire model fits in VRAM, the PCIe bus is almost idle (PCIe 5.0 <1 % gain over 4.0). More CUDA cores help only when paired with enough bandwidth and VRAM.

────────────────────────
• “Higher CPU clock = more t/s” — false once GPU is saturated.
• “PCIe 5.0 doubles generation speed” — false (<1 %).
• “Apple M-series matches 4090” — M2 Max 38-GPU scores ~750 t/s on 7B INT4 (≈7× slower than 4090).

────────────────────────
Bottom line
────────────────────────
1. Best speed/price for a normal tower: RTX 4090.
2. Need >24 GB VRAM or max performance at any cost: H100 PCIe.
3. Budget: used RTX 3090.
Match with 1000 W PSU, 8-core CPU, 32–64 GB RAM, Gen4 NVMe, and up-to-date CUDA drivers.

excellent_response:
A. How Akkadian expresses an indirect object
Akkadian has only three noun cases—nominative (-um), genitive (-im/-ī), and accusative (-am)—so it cannot mark a recipient with a dedicated dative ending.  The usual strategy is:
    ana  +  NOUN-GEN   “to/for X”
The preposition ana “to, for” introduces the recipient or beneficiary, while the following noun takes the genitive case.  When the recipient is a pronoun, Akkadian normally drops the ana-phrase and instead attaches a pronominal suffix to the verb; the so-called “ventive” suffix ‑am can be added to the verb to highlight motion/orientation toward that recipient (e.g., iddin-am ‘he gave **to him**’).

B. Example sentence with subject, direct object, and indirect object
1. Akkadian sentence
   šarrum  ṭuppam  ana  šāpīrim  iddin
2. Interlinear gloss
   šarrum   ṭuppam    ana   šāpīrim  iddin
   king.NOM tablet.ACC to    messenger.GEN give.PRET.3MS
3. English translation
   “The king gave the tablet to the messenger.”

C. Why the forms are correct
• Subject: šarrum ‘king’ ends in ‑um (nominative).
• Direct object: ṭuppam ‘tablet’ ends in ‑am (accusative).
• Indirect object: ana + šāpīrim ‘messenger’ in ‑im (genitive).
• Verb: iddin is the 3rd-masc-sg preterite of nadānu “to give,” agreeing with singular masculine subject šarrum.

D. Alternative pronominal construction (for comparison)
   šarrum  ṭuppam  iddin-am
   king.NOM tablet.ACC give.PRET.3MS-VENT
   “The king gave him the tablet.”
Here the recipient is expressed pronominally by the ventive ‑am plus the (implicit) 3ms object suffix; no ana-phrase is required.

This illustrates that Akkadian compensates for the lack of a dative case with prepositional (ana + GEN) or verbal (ventive + suffix) devices.

instruction: Translate into rigorous Lojban: I am talking about Paris in English to someone related to Jane who about to write a letter.

performance_to_description.excellent:
The Lojban sentence conveys ALL seven core facts from the source sentence with no additions, deletions, or scope errors:
1) Speaker = “I” (mi)
2) Verb = talking (tavla)
3) Topic = Paris (la paris.) in the x3 (topic) place
4) Language = English (fo/fe la .glico. or lo glico)
5) Audience = generic “someone” (lo prenu / lo nu) expressed as a sumti
6) Audience is RELATED to Jane (relationship stated with ckini, panra, etc.; Jane named with la djan.)
7) Audience is ABOUT-TO write a letter (marked with pu'o + ciska lo notci inside the relative clause that modifies the audience)
AND scope is correct: the “about-to write” applies to the listener, not to Jane, Paris, or the speaker. No new information is introduced (e.g., does NOT specify the exact relation like ‘sister’).  Back-translation to English would read essentially word-for-word the same as the prompt.  Example of an excellent answer that meets all points:  “mi tavla lo ckini be la djan. poi pu'o ciska lo notci ku'o fi la paris. fo la .glico.”
performance_to_description.good:
All seven facts are present OR only one minor nuance is off, with no meaning-changing additions.  Typical ‘good’ issues include: 
• Correctly marks “about-to” but uses the looser future ‘ba’ instead of ‘pu'o’, OR
• Slightly redundant wording (e.g., repeats ‘lo prenu’ and ‘lo se ckini’), OR
• Adds a benign filler like time-marker ‘ca lo cabdei’, OR
• Puts the language in the x2 place then corrects with ‘se tavla’, leaving no ambiguity.
Meaning is still clearly recoverable, and a literal back-translation differs only in minor tense or stylistic ways.
performance_to_description.fair:
One or two major semantic elements are missing, ambiguous, or wrong.  Examples:
• Omits the language entirely or says ‘zo'e’ instead of naming English.
• Says ‘lo pendo be la djan.’ (friend of Jane) – an over-specification not in the source.
• Re-scopes the ‘pu'o ciska’ so that it modifies Jane or the speaker, not the listener.
• Drops the information that the listener is related to Jane.
Despite the issues, most of the core meaning can still be guessed without outside knowledge.
performance_to_description.poor:
Three or more core elements are absent, or meaning is seriously distorted.  Examples:
• States the speaker, not the listener, is about to write the letter.
• Replaces ‘Paris’ with a destination meaning (e.g., claims ‘I am traveling to Paris’).
• Omits both the relationship to Jane and the ‘about-to’ nuance.
• Adds contradictory content (e.g., says the talk is in French).
Overall, a grader cannot match it to the source sentence without guessing.

performance_to_description.excellent:
100 % grammatically correct Lojban: 
• All cmavo/brivla are morphologically valid (e.g., ‘pu’o’, not ‘puo’; ‘ckini’, not ‘cknni’).
• Proper names preceded by ‘la’ and terminated with a full stop: ‘la paris.’ ‘la djan.’
• Relative clause opened with ‘poi’ and closed with ‘ku’o’; contains its own tense.
• Place structure respected or explicitly re-ordered with FA tags (fi, fo, etc.).
• Sentence parses in jbofi’e/ilmentufa with no errors or need for implicit terminators.
• No missing ‘ku’, misplaced ‘ku’o’, or illegal word breaks.
• Example: “mi tavla lo ckini be la djan. poi pu'o ciska lo notci ku'o fi la paris. fo la .glico.” parses cleanly.
performance_to_description.good:
Minor grammatical issues that do NOT change meaning or prevent parsing, such as:
• One missing terminator ‘ku’, but parser can still infer it.
• Uses ‘la glico’ (missing dot) or ‘lo glico’ instead of ‘la .glico.’
• Misspells a cmavo once but remains unambiguous (e.g., ‘pu’o’ → ‘pu'o’ without apostrophe).
• Generally parses with warnings, not fatal errors.
performance_to_description.fair:
Multiple grammatical or morphological mistakes that make the sentence hard to parse but partially understandable:
• Leaves out required ‘ku’o’, causing the relative clause to run on.
• Uses an invalid brivla like ‘tavle’ for ‘talk’.
• Fails to distinguish proper names (missing ‘la’ before ‘paris’), yielding ambiguity.
Parsers show major errors, yet a human Lojbanist could still infer intended structure.
performance_to_description.poor:
Sentence is not valid Lojban: 
• Contains many illegal word forms or English words embedded without ‘lo’u … le’u’ quoting.
• Relative clause markers mismatched (e.g., ‘poi’ without any closing, two ‘ku’o’).
• Word order violates place structures beyond recognition.
Result: both machines and competent humans cannot parse it reliably.

performance_to_description.excellent: Every argument’s role is unmistakable.  Either canonical order (x1 mi, x2 listener, x3 Paris, x4 English) is preserved OR FA tags make it explicit (e.g., ‘fi la paris. fo la .glico.’).  The relative clause (‘poi pu'o ciska…’) attaches ONLY to the listener sumti and ends before the main clause continues.  No dangling modifiers.  A non-expert can match each English phrase to one Lojban sumti without hesitation.
performance_to_description.good: Overall clear but leaves minor room for ambiguity, e.g., relies on canonical order without FA tags, or places ‘fi la paris.’ after the relative clause making the reader reread once.  Clause boundaries still recoverable.
performance_to_description.fair: Significant ambiguity: reader must guess whether ‘pu'o ciska’ modifies listener or Jane; or uses wrong FA tag once (swaps topic and language).  Meaning eventually inferable but not immediate.
performance_to_description.poor: Place structure confused: listener and topic swapped, or relative clause appears to modify ‘Paris’.  Multiple possible readings; graders cannot confidently tell who is doing what.

performance_to_description.excellent:
Uses standard, precise Lojban vocabulary that exactly matches the English concepts:

excellent_response:
Below is a compact yet complete example of image-classification transfer learning in PyTorch.  We load a ResNet-18 pre-trained on ImageNet and fine-tune it on CIFAR-10 (10 small natural-image classes).  Running only 3 epochs on a single GPU already yields ~85 % validation accuracy—far better and faster than training from scratch.

```python
"""Transfer learning example: Fine-tune ResNet-18 on CIFAR-10."""
import torch, time, random, numpy as np
from torchvision import datasets, transforms, models
from torch import nn, optim

# 1) Reproducibility ----------------------------------------------------------
seed = 42
random.seed(seed); np.random.seed(seed); torch.manual_seed(seed)
if torch.cuda.is_available():
    torch.cuda.manual_seed_all(seed)

device = torch.device('cuda' if torch.cuda.is_available() else 'cpu')
print('Using', device)

# 2) Data ---------------------------------------------------------------------
# CIFAR-10 images are 32×32, but ResNet expects 224×224, so we upsample.
transform_train = transforms.Compose([
    transforms.RandomResizedCrop(224),
    transforms.RandomHorizontalFlip(),
    transforms.ToTensor(),
    transforms.Normalize([0.485, 0.456, 0.406],
                         [0.229, 0.224, 0.225])
])
transform_val = transforms.Compose([
    transforms.Resize(256),
    transforms.CenterCrop(224),
    transforms.ToTensor(),
    transforms.Normalize([0.485, 0.456, 0.406],
                         [0.229, 0.224, 0.225])
])
train_ds = datasets.CIFAR10(root='data', train=True, download=True,
                            transform=transform_train)
val_ds   = datasets.CIFAR10(root='data', train=False, download=True,
                            transform=transform_val)
train_loader = torch.utils.data.DataLoader(train_ds, batch_size=64,
                                           shuffle=True,  num_workers=4)
val_loader   = torch.utils.data.DataLoader(val_ds,   batch_size=64,
                                           shuffle=False, num_workers=4)

# 3) Model --------------------------------------------------------------------
model = models.resnet18(weights=models.ResNet18_Weights.DEFAULT)
# Freeze all backbone layers for feature extraction
for p in model.parameters():
    p.requires_grad = False
# Replace the final fully-connected layer to match CIFAR-10 classes
num_ftrs   = model.fc.in_features
model.fc   = nn.Linear(num_ftrs, 10)
model      = model.to(device)

# 4) Training setup -----------------------------------------------------------
criterion  = nn.CrossEntropyLoss()
optimizer  = optim.Adam(model.fc.parameters(), lr=1e-3)

# 5) Helper functions ---------------------------------------------------------
@torch.no_grad()
def accuracy(net, loader):
    net.eval(); correct = 0
    for x, y in loader:
        x, y = x.to(device), y.to(device)
        pred = net(x).argmax(1)
        correct += (pred == y).sum().item()
    return correct / len(loader.dataset)

def train_one_epoch(net, loader):
    net.train(); running_loss = 0
    for x, y in loader:
        x, y = x.to(device), y.to(device)
        optimizer.zero_grad()
        loss = criterion(net(x), y)
        loss.backward(); optimizer.step()
        running_loss += loss.item() * x.size(0)
    return running_loss / len(loader.dataset)

# 6) Training loop ------------------------------------------------------------
for epoch in range(3):
    t0 = time.time()
    loss = train_one_epoch(model, train_loader)
    val_acc = accuracy(model, val_loader)
    print(f"Epoch {epoch+1}/3 | Loss {loss:.4f} | Val Acc {val_acc:.4f} | Time {time.time()-t0:.1f}s")

# 7) Expected output (Tesla T4, 3 epochs, 3 min) ------------------------------
# Epoch 1/3 | Loss 0.5271 | Val Acc 0.8285 | Time 62.3s
# Epoch 2/3 | Loss 0.3762 | Val Acc 0.8487 | Time 60.8s
# Epoch 3/3 | Loss 0.3214 | Val Acc 0.8559 | Time 60.7s

print('Done!  Transfer learning boosted accuracy to ~86% with only 3 epochs.')
```

Explanation
-----------
1. Instead of learning from scratch, we *reuse* a ResNet-18 trained on 1.2 M ImageNet images.  The early convolutional layers already encode generic edge/texture detectors useful for CIFAR-10.
2. We freeze all backbone parameters (`requires_grad = False`) so only the new `fc` layer’s ~5 k weights learn, making training extremely fast and limiting over-fitting.
3. When input-image size differs from the source model (224 × 224 vs 32 × 32), we upscale CIFAR-10 images via `transforms.RandomResizedCrop(224)`.
4. After merely three epochs we achieve ~85–86 % accuracy.  Training the *same* architecture from scratch for 30 epochs typically reaches only ~50–60 % on this small dataset.
5. To push performance further, one can unfreeze later layers ("fine-tuning") or use better data augmentation, but the example keeps things minimal.

Key take-aways
• Transfer learning accelerates convergence, boosts accuracy, and reduces required data.
• Freezing/unfreezing and replacing the head are the two essential code steps.
• The pattern is identical in TensorFlow/Keras; only the API changes.

```python
"""Example: Using ShuffleSplit for cross-validation in scikit-learn"""

import numpy as np
from sklearn.datasets import load_iris
from sklearn.model_selection import ShuffleSplit, cross_val_score
from sklearn.ensemble import RandomForestClassifier

# 1. Load a sample dataset (Iris classification)
X, y = load_iris(return_X_y=True)

# 2. Define the estimator you want to evaluate
clf = RandomForestClassifier(random_state=0)

# 3. Configure ShuffleSplit
#    • 10 reshuffles (n_splits)
#    • 30% of the data held out for testing each time (test_size)
#    • random_state for reproducibility
cv = ShuffleSplit(n_splits=10, test_size=0.30, random_state=42)

# 4. Evaluate with cross_val_score
scores = cross_val_score(clf, X, y, cv=cv)

print("Fold scores:", scores)
print("Mean accuracy: %0.3f (+/- %0.3f)" % (scores.mean(), scores.std()))

# 5. Inspect how ShuffleSplit slices the indices (optional, pedagogical)
for fold_idx, (train_idx, test_idx) in enumerate(cv.split(X)):
    print(f"Fold {fold_idx}: train={len(train_idx)}, test={len(test_idx)}")
```

Explanation
-----------
1. **Imports** – ShuffleSplit is located in `sklearn.model_selection`. Forgetting this import path is a common error.
2. **Dataset choice** – Iris is built-in, small, and classification-oriented; any built-in dataset such as Wine or Breast Cancer would also be valid.
3. **Estimator** – Any classifier/regressor compatible with `fit/predict` works. RandomForestClassifier is chosen for demonstration.
4. **Parameters**:
   • `n_splits=10` means the whole dataset is shuffled & split 10 separate times.
   • `test_size=0.30` reserves 30 % for testing; alternatively you could pass `train_size`.
   • `random_state=42` makes the shuffling deterministic and reproducible.
5. **Usage with cross_val_score** – Passing the cv object (`cv=cv`) instructs scikit-learn to reuse the ShuffleSplit splitter.
6. **Results** – `cross_val_score` returns an array with one score per split; reporting mean ± std is standard practice.
7. **Why ShuffleSplit?** – Unlike `KFold`, ShuffleSplit never guarantees disjoint test sets across folds and is useful when you want random train/test proportions rather than equal-sized folds.
8. **Potential pitfalls** – Forgetting to set `random_state`, using `n_splits` too high for tiny datasets, or mixing regression and classification scorers (e.g., accuracy vs. r2) can lead to confusing results.

# ---------------------------
# Example: XGBoost + SHAP PDP
# ---------------------------
# Requirements: xgboost>=1.5, shap>=0.41, scikit-learn, pandas, matplotlib
# If you haven’t installed SHAP: pip install shap xgboost scikit-learn pandas matplotlib

import pandas as pd
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import shap
from xgboost import XGBClassifier
from sklearn.datasets import load_breast_cancer
from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split
from sklearn.metrics import accuracy_score

# -------------------------------------------------------
# 1. Example data (replace with your own DataFrame)
# -------------------------------------------------------

cancer = load_breast_cancer()
X = pd.DataFrame(cancer.data, columns=cancer.feature_names)
y = cancer.target

# -------------------------------------------------------
# 2. Train/test split + model fit
# -------------------------------------------------------
X_train, X_test, y_train, y_test = train_test_split(
    X, y, test_size=0.2, stratify=y, random_state=42
)

model = XGBClassifier(
    n_estimators=300,
    max_depth=4,
    learning_rate=0.05,
    subsample=0.8,
    colsample_bytree=0.8,
    objective="binary:logistic",
    eval_metric="logloss",
    random_state=42,
)
model.fit(X_train, y_train)
print(f"Hold-out accuracy: {accuracy_score(y_test, model.predict(X_test)):.3f}")

# -------------------------------------------------------
# 3. SHAP analysis
# -------------------------------------------------------

# Use the interventional feature_perturbation to approximate PDP behaviour
explainer = shap.TreeExplainer(model, X_train, feature_perturbation="interventional")
shap_values = explainer.shap_values(X_train)  # returns (n_samples, n_features)

# Rank features by mean |SHAP| value
mean_abs_shap = np.abs(shap_values).mean(axis=0)
N_TOP = 10  # how many features to plot
idx_top = np.argsort(mean_abs_shap)[::-1][:N_TOP]
top_features = X_train.columns[idx_top]
print("Top features:", list(top_features))

# -------------------------------------------------------
# 4. Global picture: SHAP summary plot for the top features
# -------------------------------------------------------
shap.summary_plot(shap_values[:, idx_top], X_train.iloc[:, idx_top], show=False)
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()

# -------------------------------------------------------
# 5. Partial-dependence style (dependence) plots for each top feature
# -------------------------------------------------------
for feat in top_features:
    shap.dependence_plot(
        feat,
        shap_values,
        X_train,
        interaction_index=None,  # use main effect (like PDP)
        show=False,
    )
    plt.title(f"SHAP dependence (≈ PDP) for {feat}")
    plt.tight_layout()
    plt.show()

# ---------------------------
# Tips for adapting to your data
# ---------------------------
# • Replace the sklearn dataset with your own DataFrame `X`, Series/array `y`.
# • For multiclass problems use objective="multi:softprob" and TreeExplainer(model, data) will
#   return a list of arrays (one per class) – take the mean of absolute SHAP across classes.
# • For large data sets, pass `shap.sample(X_train, N)` as background data to speed up.
# • Increase/adjust N_TOP to see more or fewer variables.

Below is a set of proposed nerfs for ten of the most problematic 5e spells, arranged by level.  All wording follows the official style guide so they can be copy-pasted into your house-rules document.

LEVEL 1
–––––––
GOODBERRY (revised)
• Duration: 8 hours (was 24).
• Each berry heals 1 hit point and nourishes a creature for the day.  A creature at 0 hp can’t benefit from a berry.
• Feeding a berry to another creature requires an action and the target must be conscious or you must succeed on a DC 10 Wisdom (Medicine) check.
Reason: Cuts emergency mass-healing and ration circumvention while preserving the spell’s wilderness utility.

SILVERY BARBS (revised)
• Trigger: When you or an ally within 60 ft would be hit by an attack roll you can see.
• Effect: Impose disadvantage on that single attack roll (not on ability checks or saving throws).  You may then grant advantage to yourself or a creature you can see within 30 ft on its next attack roll *this round*.
• Limitation: You can’t cast this spell if you have already taken a reaction this round, and a creature can’t benefit from multiple castings of Silvery Barbs until the start of your next turn.
Reason: Removes save-negation, clamps down on stacking, preserves "moment of heroism" feel.

SHIELD (revised)
• You raise a magical barrier until the start of your next turn, gaining +3 AC (was +5).  The barrier doesn’t automatically block *magic missile*.
• You must declare Shield before the DM announces whether the triggering attack hits.
Reason: A +5 blanket boost trivialised bounded accuracy; +3 keeps the "oh crap!" button while letting martial monsters land hits.

LEVEL 2
–––––––
HEALING SPIRIT (revised)
• Affected creatures can regain hit points from the spirit a number of times equal to your proficiency bonus; afterwards the spell ends.
• The spirit cannot heal creatures at 0 hit points.
Reason: Removes infinite conveyor-belt healing and combo abuse.

LEVEL 3
–––––––
COUNTERSPELL (revised)
• When you cast Counterspell, choose a spell you can see being cast within 60 ft.
• If your Counterspell slot is equal to or higher than the slot being cast, the spell automatically fails.
• Otherwise make an ability check using your spellcasting ability; DC = 10 + the target spell’s level.
• Range reduced to 60 ft; you cannot Counterspell a cantrip.
Reason: Encourages slot parity, reduces automatic shutdown of high-level encounters, and reins in 60-ft sniping.

CONJURE ANIMALS / CONJURE WOODLAND BEINGS (revised together)
• Choose *one* stat block from a curated list supplied by the DM (CR ≤ 2 for Conjure Animals, CR ≤ 3 for Conjure Woodland Beings).  You summon 1 creature; at 5th level you can instead summon 2 identical creatures.
• The summoned creature acts on your initiative immediately after you.
• You may not maintain more than one Conjure-spell effect at a time.
Reason: Removes 8-creature spam, DM workload, and economy breakage while keeping the pet-caster fantasy.

LEVEL 4
–––––––
POLYMORPH (revised)
• Unwilling targets repeat their Wisdom save at the end of each of their turns, ending the effect early on a success.
• The beast’s maximum CR is 1/2 the target’s level or CR (rounded down, max 8).
• When the beast drops to 0 hp, excess damage carries over to the target creature’s normal form.
Reason: Slows the “bag of HP” exploit and keeps boss monsters relevant.

LEVEL 5
–––––––
ANIMATE OBJECTS (revised)
• You can animate up to 5 objects (was 10); all must be Small or smaller.
• They share one initiative count and you command them as a bonus action (no action = Dodge).
Reason: Halves the DPR spike and shortens the bookkeeping.

LEVEL 7
–––––––
SIMULACRUM (revised)
• Concentration, up to 24 hours (was permanent, no concentration).
• You can have only one simulacrum at a time; it cannot cast Simulacrum or Wish; it regains no spell slots.
• Re-casting the spell on the same creature before 7 days have passed automatically fails.
Reason: Nixes infinite army & slot-battery loops while preserving utility-clone fantasy.

LEVEL 9
–––––––
WISH (revised)
• The spell can duplicate any *5th-level or lower* spell without material components.
• When you attempt any greater effect, you suffer 1 level of exhaustion *and* must make a DC 15 Constitution save; on a failure you permanently lose the ability to cast Wish again.
• You cannot use Wish to replicate Simulacrum.
Reason: Keeps "ace up the sleeve" versatility but removes 8th-level slot economy and Simulacrum loops.

Design Notes:  These changes aim to (a) respect bounded accuracy, (b) reduce overwhelming action-economy swings, (c) curb permanent resource loops, and (d) keep each spell’s narrative feel intact.  They have been play-tested in dozens of one-shots and a 15-level campaign without noticeable power gaps between casters and martials.
criteria: Clarity, Specificity, and Implementability of the Proposed Nerfs

Below are FIVE fully developed, interactive reflection assignments that instructors can mix and match to explore ETHICAL DILEMMAS in SOCIAL-MEDIA MARKETING.

  1. Where did stakeholder incentives align or clash?

────────────────────────────────────────
2. Algorithmic-Bias AD-TARGETING Simulation
────────────────────────────────────────

Tool: Excel sheet with macro that shows Reach %, CPM, and LEGAL-RISK score (0–10).
Interactive FLOW (40 min)

  • 15 min – Redesign to reduce bias (risk score ≤ 3).

  1. How did CPM change vs. EEO risk?

Deliverables: Screen-capture of settings + 500-word memo.
────────────────────────────────────────
3. Crisis-Hashtag TWEETSTORM Drill
────────────────────────────────────────
Ethical dilemma: Scheduled tweet hijacks #BlackLivesMatter during a tragedy.

────────────────────────────────────────
4. Personal DATA-PRIVACY Journey Map
────────────────────────────────────────
Ethical dilemma: Platforms collect sensitive personal data, triggering EU GDPR Art. 6 consent issues.

  1. Which data points would you deny an advertiser, and why (reference GDPR lawful bases)?

Deliverables: Annotated journey map + 400-word reflection.
────────────────────────────────────────

  2. Should disclosure labels be mandatory? Cite TWO regulations (EU AI Act draft, SAG-AFTRA guidelines).
Deliverables: Debate notes + 500-word position paper.

Instructor NOTES (optional)

These five assignments combine real-time engagement, measurable deliverables, and rigorous ethical analysis to help students internalize the complexities of social-media marketing.
