instruction: Can you write a haskell function that solves the two sum problem, where the inputs are a vector of numbers and a target number. The function should return the two numbers in the array that some to the target number or return -1 if an answer is not found in the array

performance_to_description.excellent:
• Code compiles with GHC 9.x with only the standard libraries shown in the answer, no edits required.
• For input V.fromList [2,7,11,15] 9 it prints Right (2,7) or Right (7,2) (numbers, not indices).
• For V.fromList [1,1,3] 2 it prints Right (1,1) – proves it can use the same value at two distinct indices.
• For V.fromList [-3,4,3,90] 0 it prints Right (-3,3) – handles negatives.
• For V.fromList [] 99 and V.singleton 42 42 it immediately returns Left (-1) (or the exact sentinel –1 if the function returns a plain Int) without crashing.
• For V.fromList [1,2,3] 100 it returns Left (-1) (or –1) – correct failure signalling.
• In every successful case x + y == target is True and each x, y occurs in the original vector at distinct positions.
• Never returns indices, tuples whose sum is wrong, or duplicates of the same element position.
• No runtime exceptions (no out-of-bounds, divide by zero, etc.).
performance_to_description.good:
• Code compiles and returns the correct pair for the canonical test [2,7,11,15]/9.
• May fail ONE of the secondary tests (e.g., duplicates OR negatives OR length<2) but still produces a valid pair for the rest.
• Always returns numbers (not indices) and never crashes.
• Produces the correct failure sentinel for at least the empty-vector case OR the no-solution case, but not necessarily both.
performance_to_description.fair:
• Code compiles but exhibits at least two functional weaknesses: may return indices instead of numbers, or succeed only on the canonical test while failing duplicates/negatives, or re-uses the same index twice.
• May crash or throw on one edge-case (e.g., empty vector) but works on non-edge inputs.
• Wrong or inconsistent failure sentinel (e.g., Nothing, [], 0) in some cases.
performance_to_description.poor:
• Does not compile OR
• Compiles but produces wrong answers on the canonical test ([2,7,11,15], 9) OR
• Crashes on normal input OR
• Returns a value of the wrong type (e.g., indices, String) so results cannot be compared.

performance_to_description.excellent:
• Code contains a single linear scan (O(n)) using a HashMap/Set or equivalent; there is no nested loop over the vector length.
• Additional memory is O(n) or less; does NOT build a list of all pairs.
• Function exits immediately once a valid pair is found (no scanning the tail after success).
• No expensive operations inside the tight loop (no repeated V.length, no repeated conversions with V.toList, no sort each step).
• Uses strict variants (e.g. Data.HashMap.Strict, foldl') to avoid space leaks, OR comments explain why laziness is safe.
• Code comments or docstring explicitly state the complexity as “O(n) time, O(n) space”.
performance_to_description.good:
• Overall complexity is acceptable (≤O(n log n)) but not optimal. Typical example: converts vector to list, sorts once, then two-pointer sweep.
• Contains at most one nested loop but the outer loop may be over a reduced set (average O(n)) so still practical.
• Some minor redundant calls inside the loop (e.g., V.length) but unlikely to blow up on vectors <10^5.
• Memory usage is still O(n) or less.
• Complexity comment present but may be incorrect OR missing strictness annotations.
performance_to_description.fair:
• Naïve O(n²) double loop clearly visible (e.g., for i in [0..n-1], for j in [i+1..n-1]).
• Converts vector to list and then, inside the fold, calls elem/lookup each time (implies O(n²)).
• No early exit; continues scanning after a pair is found.
• No statement of complexity OR claims O(n) when implementation is obviously quadratic.
performance_to_description.poor:
• Infinite or exponential behaviour (e.g., recursively enumerating power-set) OR
• Repeatedly sorts or rebuilds large structures inside loops OR
• Evident resource blow-up (e.g., stores every possible pair in memory) OR
• Grader cannot determine complexity because code does not compile.

performance_to_description.excellent:
• Provides an explicit, general type signature such as (Eq a, Num a) => V.Vector a -> a -> Either Int (a, a).
• Behaviour matches the signature (uses Left (-1) for failure, Right (x,y) for success).
• Uses Data.Vector (boxed or unboxed) directly; no unsafe indexing without bounds check.
• Avoids all partial functions (head, tail, (!!), fromJust) or guards against empty cases first.
• Compiles with -Wall -Werror: no warnings about incomplete patterns, unused imports, or defaulting.
• Imports are minimal and qualified (e.g., import qualified Data.HashMap.Strict as HM).
• Employs idiomatic constructs: pattern matching, guards, foldl', where-clauses instead of mutable loops.
• No use of error, undefined, or unsafePerformIO.
performance_to_description.good:
• Type signature present but slightly less general (e.g., Int instead of polymorphic) OR returns Maybe instead of Either yet still documents it.
• One or two benign warnings remain (e.g., "redundant import").
• Uses one partial function but in a context where it is safe (e.g., head after checking length>0).
• Imports somewhat verbose but reasonable.
• Mostly idiomatic but has minor imperative or non-idiomatic bits (e.g., whileM loop from Control.Monad).
performance_to_description.fair:
• No top-level type signature OR signature mismatches implementation.
• Frequent partial functions without checks.
• Converts vector to list for convenience (loses performance and idiomatic advantage).
• Multiple compiler warnings, but still compiles.
• Uses error/undefined for impossible cases.
performance_to_description.poor:

{-# LANGUAGE ScopedTypeVariables #-}
import qualified Data.Vector         as V
import qualified Data.HashMap.Strict as HM
import           Data.Either         (Either(..))

-- | twoSum takes a vector of numeric values and a target.
--   On success it returns Right (x, y) where x + y == target
--   and x and y are elements from the original vector.
--   If no such pair exists it returns Left (-1).
--
--   Complexity:  O(n) time,  O(n) additional space.
--   Example: twoSum (V.fromList [2,7,11,15]) 9  ==> Right (2,7)
--            twoSum (V.fromList [1]) 2          ==> Left (-1)

twoSum :: (Eq a, Num a, Ord a) => V.Vector a -> a -> Either Int (a, a)
twoSum vec target = maybe (Left (-1)) Right $ go 0 HM.empty
  where
    len = V.length vec

    go i seen
      | i >= len  = Nothing                                 -- scanned whole vector
      | otherwise =
          let x      = vec V.! i
              needed = target - x
          in case HM.lookup needed seen of
               Just _  -> Just (x, needed)                  -- found the complement
               Nothing -> go (i + 1) (HM.insert x () seen) -- keep looking

-- Quick manual tests
main :: IO ()
main = do
  let v1 = V.fromList [2,7,11,15]
  print $ twoSum v1 9          -- Right (2,7)

  let v2 = V.fromList [1,1,3]
  print $ twoSum v2 2          -- Right (1,1)

  let v3 = V.fromList [-3,4,3,90]
  print $ twoSum v3 0          -- Right (-3,3)

  let v4 = V.singleton 5
  print $ twoSum v4 5          -- Left (-1)

  let v5 = V.fromList [1,2,3]
  print $ twoSum v5 100        -- Left (-1)

def solve_quadratic(a: float, b: float, c: float, *, complex_solutions: bool = True):
    """Return the two roots of ax^2 + bx + c = 0.

    Parameters
    ----------
    a, b, c : float or int
        Coefficients of the quadratic equation.
    complex_solutions : bool, default True
        If True, allow complex solutions using ``cmath`` when the
        discriminant is negative.  If False, raise a ValueError when
        the equation has no real roots.

    Returns
    -------
    tuple(root1, root2)
        The two roots. If the roots are identical (discriminant == 0),
        the value will be repeated, e.g. (-1.0, -1.0).

    Raises
    ------
    ValueError
        If `a` is zero (not a quadratic) or if `complex_solutions` is
        False and the discriminant is negative.

    Examples
    --------
    >>> solve_quadratic(1, -3, 2)
    (2.0, 1.0)
    >>> solve_quadratic(1, 2, 1)
    (-1.0, -1.0)
    >>> solve_quadratic(1, 0, 1, complex_solutions=False)
    Traceback (most recent call last):
        ...
    ValueError: Equation has no real roots.
    """

    import cmath, math

    # Validate coefficients
    for name, coef in zip(("a", "b", "c"), (a, b, c)):
        if not isinstance(coef, (int, float)):
            raise TypeError(f"Coefficient '{name}' must be a number, got {type(coef).__name__}.")

    if a == 0:
        raise ValueError("Coefficient 'a' must be non-zero for a quadratic equation.")

    # Compute discriminant
    D = b * b - 4 * a * c

    # Select sqrt function
    root_calc = cmath.sqrt if (D < 0 and complex_solutions) else math.sqrt

    if D < 0 and not complex_solutions:
        raise ValueError("Equation has no real roots.")

    sqrt_D = root_calc(D)

    # Numerically stable quadratic formula
    if b >= 0:
        q = -0.5 * (b + sqrt_D)
    else:
        q = -0.5 * (b - sqrt_D)

    x1 = q / a
    x2 = c / q if q != 0 else x1  # Handles repeated root

    return (x1, x2)


if __name__ == "__main__":
    # Sanity tests
    assert solve_quadratic(1, -3, 2) == (2.0, 1.0)
    assert solve_quadratic(1, 2, 1) == (-1.0, -1.0)
    r1, r2 = solve_quadratic(1, 0, 1)
    assert abs(r1.real) < 1e-12 and abs(r1.imag - 1) < 1e-12
    print("All tests passed.")

Thank you for coming in today. I’m glad your vitals and exam are normal. Still, chest or upper-abdominal pain always deserves a careful look. Here is how I would proceed:

1. Clarify the history
   • Location & radiation – Is the pain dead center behind the breastbone, left-sided, right-sided, or more in the pit of the stomach? Does it move to the back, shoulder, or jaw?
   • Onset & timing – When did it start? Was it sudden or gradual? Constant or intermittent? Any nighttime awakening?
   • Quality – Sharp, burning, pressure-like, stabbing?
   • Severity & trajectory – Has it been getting better, worse, or unchanged?
   • Triggers & relievers – Does food, exertion, deep breathing, body position, or antacids change it?
   • Associated symptoms – Shortness of breath, palpitations, dizziness, sweating, cough, fever, nausea, vomiting, black/tarry stools, heartburn, anxiety?
   • Past history – Asthma, reflux, ulcer disease, gallstones, heart or clotting problems, recent trauma or illness?
   • Social – Smoking, vaping, alcohol, energy drinks, recreational drugs (especially cocaine), recent long travel, heavy lifting, stress.
   • Family – Early heart disease, sudden cardiac death, clotting disorders, GI disease.
   • Medications – Exact dose of acetaminophen; any NSAIDs, supplements, or new meds.

2. Focused exam
   • Repeat vitals if pain changes.
   • Palpate costochondral joints, chest wall, and epigastrium.
   • Assess for reproducible pain vs visceral pain.

3. Preliminary differential
   Common/benign:
   • Gastroesophageal reflux disease (GERD) / dyspepsia
   • Gastritis or peptic ulcer (especially with frequent acetaminophen or NSAID use)
   • Costochondritis or muscle strain
   • Anxiety or panic attacks
   Less common but must not miss:
   • Myocardial ischemia/variant angina (rare at 19 but possible with drugs or congenital issues)
   • Pericarditis or myocarditis (post-viral)
   • Spontaneous pneumothorax
   • Pulmonary embolism (if risk factors)
   • Pneumonia/pleuritis
   • Aortic dissection (extremely rare but catastrophic)

4. Immediate work-up today (in clinic or urgent care setting)
   • 12-lead ECG – inexpensive, quick screen for ST-changes, pericarditis pattern.
   • Point-of-care troponin if ECG abnormal or strong suspicion.
   • Chest X-ray if pleuritic, respiratory, or traumatic features.
   • Basic labs (CBC, CMP, lipase) and H. pylori stool antigen if epigastric focus.

5. Initial management (assuming benign work-up)
   • Trial of proton-pump inhibitor such as omeprazole 20 mg daily for 4–8 weeks.
   • Limit acetaminophen to ≤3,000 mg (3 g) per 24 h; avoid NSAIDs while stomach is irritated.
   • Encourage small, low-fat meals; avoid caffeine, alcohol, spicy food; don’t lie flat within 2 h of eating.
   • Gentle stretching, heat, or topical NSAID gel if chest wall muscle strain suspected.
   • Stress-reduction techniques, regular sleep, physical activity.

6. Red-flag / return-immediately instructions
   Go to the emergency department (or call 911) for any of the following:
   • Chest pain that is crushing, lasts >10 min at rest, or radiates to jaw/left arm.
   • Shortness of breath, fainting, palpitations, or irregular heartbeat.
   • Vomiting blood, black stools, or severe abdominal pain.
   • Sudden worsening of pain, fever >38.5 °C, or coughing up blood.

7. Follow-up
   • Recheck in clinic in 1–2 weeks; sooner if symptoms persist or worsen.
   • If no response to PPI after 4 weeks, consider urea breath test for H. pylori, upper endoscopy, or referral to GI.

Please remember this information is educational and not a substitute for direct medical care. Let’s make sure you feel safe to ask any questions.

performance_to_description.fair: Multiple inaccuracies or outdated statements that do not endanger safety (e.g., says "borderline hypertension" for 158/120), or mixes up some pathophysiology. Still >50 % of content remains correct.
performance_to_description.poor: Contains major errors (e.g., calls 158/120 “normal BP”, recommends dangerous drug dosing), misclassifies diseases, or presents fabricated statistics obviously outside clinical reality.

performance_to_description.excellent: Advises prompt follow-up with a physician, lists at least two red-flag symptoms warranting urgent review (e.g., severe headache, visual changes, oedema, dysuria). Gives evidence-based lifestyle advice with numeric targets (e.g., sodium <2 g/day, weight loss 5–10 %, limit evening caffeine/alcohol). Avoids endorsing unproven supplements or self-medication.
performance_to_description.good: Includes recommendation to see a doctor and some lifestyle tips but without numeric specifics or red-flag list.
performance_to_description.fair: Vague reassurance without concrete safety/lifestyle guidance, or suggests unproven but harmless remedies (e.g., herbal tea).
performance_to_description.poor: Gives potentially harmful advice (e.g., “adjust your own antihypertensive doses”) or omits safety considerations entirely.

performance_to_description.excellent: Uses clear headings (e.g., “Suggested Diagnostic Work-up”, “Prognosis”), bullet points, and concise language free of unexplained jargon. Directly addresses BOTH requested items (tests *and* prognosis). No irrelevant tangents or repetition. Tone is professional and reassuring.
performance_to_description.good: Generally well organised but minor issues (one long paragraph or an unexplained acronym). Still addresses both parts of the prompt.
performance_to_description.fair: Noticeably disorganised (long blocks of text), some jargon, or partially misses either tests or prognosis.
performance_to_description.poor: Disjointed, difficult to read, or largely off-topic; fails to answer one or both parts of the question.

excellent_response:
**Suggested Diagnostic Work-up**

1. Basic Laboratory Panel  
• **Urinalysis + urine culture** – check for urinary-tract infection, haematuria, or proteinuria that can provoke nocturia.  
• **Serum creatinine, eGFR, BUN, electrolytes** – assess renal function; long-standing hypertension may cause hypertensive nephropathy that presents with nocturia.  
• **Urine albumin-to-creatinine ratio (ACR)** – early marker of chronic kidney disease (CKD).  
• **Fasting plasma glucose & HbA1c** – screen for diabetes mellitus; osmotic diuresis leads to night-time urination.  
• **Lipid profile** – cardiovascular risk stratification.

2. Cardiovascular / Blood-pressure Assessment  
• **24-hour ambulatory BP monitoring** – confirm stage 2 hypertension (average ≥160/100) and detect nocturnal non-dipping patterns that worsen renal outcomes.  
• **ECG ± echocardiography** – look for left-ventricular hypertrophy or early heart failure, which can cause nocturnal diuresis from fluid redistribution.  
• **NT-proBNP** if heart failure suspected.

3. Urological Evaluation (male patient)  
• **Post-void residual volume** (bladder scan) & **renal/bladder ultrasonography** – assess for outflow obstruction or structural disease.  
• **Serum PSA and digital rectal exam** – rule out benign prostatic hyperplasia (BPH) or other prostatic pathology.

4. Sleep & Respiratory Assessment  
• **Overnight polysomnography** – obesity and resistant hypertension raise suspicion for obstructive sleep apnoea (OSA); OSA increases atrial natriuretic peptide, leading to nocturia.

5. Targeted Tests as Indicated  
• **Thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH)** for hypothyroidism-related fluid retention.  
• **Urine specific gravity/osmolality** if diabetes insipidus is on the differential.

**Interpretation & Immediate Management**  
Abnormal findings will direct therapy: ACE-inhibitor and statin for micro-albuminuria, CPAP for OSA, alpha-blocker for BPH, intensive glycaemic control for diabetes.

**Lifestyle Advice & Safety**  
• Weight reduction of **≥10 %** and **sodium intake <2 g/day** can lower BP and nocturia frequency.  
• Restrict caffeine/alcohol after 6 PM, maintain good sleep hygiene, elevate legs before bedtime if oedematous.  
• Seek urgent care for **severe headache, visual changes, chest pain, ankle swelling, dysuria, or BP ≥180/120 mmHg**.

**Prognosis**  
• **Short-term:** Nocturia usually improves within weeks once the primary cause (e.g., UTI, BPH) is treated and BP begins to fall.  
• **Long-term, if uncontrolled:** A BP of 158/120 mmHg plus BMI ≈39 kg/m² confers a **>20 % 10-year stroke risk**, **>15 % myocardial-infarction risk**, and ~25 % chance of progressing to stage 3 CKD.  
• **If treated:** Achieving BP <130/80, HbA1c <7 %, ACR normalisation, and sustained weight loss can cut cardiovascular risk by **≥50 %** and halt CKD progression.  
Thus prognosis is **good** provided the patient engages in follow-up, adopts lifestyle changes, and any discovered conditions (e.g., diabetes, OSA) are managed promptly.

*This information is educational; final decisions rest with the treating physician after full clinical assessment.*

instruction:
Scenario:
You are the manager of a small team working on a project with tight deadlines. One of your team members consistently submits work that is below the expected quality. The team's success depends on the contributions of each member, and this individual's work is affecting overall performance. However, you know that this team member is dealing with personal challenges outside of work.

Question:
How would you approach this situation as a manager? Consider the ethical implications, team dynamics, and the need to address both the project's success and the well-being of your team member. What steps would you take to ensure a fair and constructive resolution to this issue?

performance_to_description.excellent:
• The answer treats the struggling employee with empathy and dignity throughout.
• It explicitly keeps the conversation private (e.g. “schedule a confidential 1-on-1” or “do not share personal details with the team”).
• It offers at least TWO concrete, realistic support options such as: referral to Employee Assistance Programme (EAP), flexible hours for 1-2 weeks, temporary workload reduction of 30-50 %, paid time off, or counselling services—naming the resource.
• It avoids prying; the manager invites the employee to share only what they are comfortable with.
• It references HR or legal policy to show the manager’s duty of care and compliance.
• No discriminatory, blaming, or shaming language appears.
Example wording that would earn “excellent”: “I’d like to understand what obstacles you’re facing; if you feel comfortable sharing. We have an EAP you can call 24/7, and we can move to a 32-hour week for the next fortnight.”
performance_to_description.good:
• Shows empathy but offers only ONE concrete support option or the option is vague (e.g. “let me know if you need help”).
• Mentions privacy but less explicitly; still keeps discussion 1-on-1.
• Does not pry or blame but may fail to cite HR/policy.
• Language remains respectful.
Example good sentence: “I understand you have personal challenges; let’s see if adjusting your workload helps.”
performance_to_description.fair:
• Briefly acknowledges personal issues but immediately pivots to performance; empathy is minimal or generic.
• Support options are unclear (e.g. “try to balance work and life better”).
• May unintentionally pressure disclosure.
• No explicit mention of confidentiality or HR.
Example fair sentence: “Tell me what’s wrong in your life so we can fix your work quality.”
performance_to_description.poor:
• Offers no empathy or dismisses personal challenges.
• Uses punitive or shaming tone, e.g., “Your problems are not my concern.”
• Suggests public discussion of the employee’s issues or forces disclosure.
• Gives zero support options or discriminates (e.g., “maybe this job isn’t for single parents”).

performance_to_description.excellent:
• States specific, measurable targets (SMART). Example: “Reduce code defect rate from 28 % to under 8 % within the next 30 days” or “meet 100 % of story-point commitments for the next 2 sprints.”
• Outlines a formal Performance Improvement Plan (PIP) or equivalent, including written documentation and a 30-day timeline.
• Provides precise monitoring steps: daily stand-ups, weekly reviews, progress dashboard.
• Includes contingency plans to protect project deadlines (e.g., reassigning two critical modules during the PIP).
• Avoids premature termination; allows chance to improve.
performance_to_description.good:
• Gives clear but partly measurable goals (e.g., “reduce errors significantly within the next month”).
• Mentions follow-up meetings but with less detail (e.g., “we’ll check in regularly”).
• Partial safeguarding of project (e.g., light task redistribution) but not explicit.
• Uses documentation but doesn’t name it a PIP.
performance_to_description.fair:
• Goals are vague (“do better”, “improve quality soon”).
• No structured plan or weak follow-up (e.g., “I’ll keep an eye on things”).
• No discussion of how project timelines stay intact.
• Talks about firing as first option or gives unlimited time with no accountability.
performance_to_description.poor:
• No performance metrics.
• Either immediately fires the employee without process OR ignores the quality issue entirely.
• No timeline, no monitoring, no mention of protecting the project.

performance_to_description.excellent:
• Explains how work will be rebalanced so others are not overburdened (e.g., reassign two high-priority tasks to senior developers and publicly acknowledge extra effort).
• Communicates changes to the team transparently yet without exposing personal details (“We’re adjusting assignments to match current capacity”).
• Identifies potential morale issues (resentment, perceived favoritism) and provides mitigation (e.g., open Q&A in next stand-up, recognition, support resources for rest of team).
• Ensures equal treatment: states that same PIP template applies to any employee.
performance_to_description.good:
• Mentions task redistribution but not in depth; or recognises extra workload informally.
• Keeps confidentiality but gives minimal explanation to team.
• Touches on morale but without concrete action.
performance_to_description.fair:
• Ignores impact on other team members OR vaguely says “others will pick up the slack.”
• Provides no plan to maintain morale.
• Risk of perceived favoritism not addressed.
performance_to_description.poor:
• Dumps additional work on team with no acknowledgement.
• Publicly shares employee’s personal problems.
• No team communication plan; fairness completely absent.

performance_to_description.excellent:
• Identifies at least two realistic resources a small team could access: HR partner, EAP, internal mentor, short training course, flexible hours.
• Steps are feasible given a tight deadline (e.g., 50 % workload reduction, not full removal).
• Mentions documenting meetings and decisions for legal compliance.
• Provides escalation path: additional training → extended PIP → possible reassignment/termination per policy.
performance_to_description.good:
• References at least one organizational resource but with limited detail.
• Actions generally realistic but some may strain a small team (e.g., suggests two-week external training without coverage).
• Documentation or escalation path mentioned briefly.
performance_to_description.fair:
• Resource suggestions are generic or unlikely (e.g., “hire three contractors” for a small team).
• Little sense of feasibility or policy.
• No clear escalation or documentation.
performance_to_description.poor:
• Suggests impossible resources (e.g., unlimited budget sabbatical) or none at all.
• No mention of documentation, policy, or escalation.

performance_to_description.excellent:
• Well-structured (logical steps or numbered list) under 450 words.
• Plain language free of jargon; each action easy to follow.
• Professional, constructive tone; no bias.
• Covers all major facets (ethics, performance, team, practicality) without rambling.
performance_to_description.good:
• Mostly clear; minor verbosity or minor use of jargon.
• Structure present but some points out of order.
• Tone appropriate.
performance_to_description.fair:
• Hard to follow: long paragraphs, missing sequence, redundant wording.
• Occasional unprofessional tone or jargon.
performance_to_description.poor:
• Disorganized, rambling, or under 50 words.
• Confusing, unhelpful, or biased language.

excellent_response:
Step 1 – Gather evidence
• Review last two sprints: Jane’s code had a 28 % rework rate vs team 5 %. Three critical bugs delayed release by 2 days.

Step 2 – Schedule confidential 1-on-1 (within 24 h)
• Private meeting room; HR policy and EAP brochure ready.

Step 3 – Conduct the meeting (empathy + clarity)
1. Thank Jane for her effort: “I appreciate what you’ve contributed.”
2. Present facts: “28 % rework compared to team average of 5 %.”
3. Invite her perspective and whether anything outside work is affecting her. Emphasise “share only what you’re comfortable with – this stays between us.”

Step 4 – Offer support
• Option A: Flexible schedule for next 2 weeks (10 am–4 pm core hours).
• Option B: Temporary 50 % ticket load.
• Option C: Contact EAP (free 24 / 7 counselling).
• Encourage use of 2 personal PTO days if needed.

Step 5 – Co-create Performance Improvement Plan
• Goal 1: Rework rate < 8 % within 30 days.
• Goal 2: Hit 100 % of story-point commitments in next 2 sprints.
• Resources: pair programming buddy, QA checklist.
• Check-ins: 15-min daily stand-up + formal review day 30.
• Written PIP signed and filed with HR.

Step 6 – Safeguard team & morale
• Reassign two critical modules to Sam and Alex; recognise their extra effort in team meeting.
• Tell team: “We’re rebalancing tasks to keep scope on track.” No personal details shared.

Step 7 – Monitor & escalate
• Weekly quality dashboard shared with Jane.
• If targets met, restore full workload and acknowledge success.
• If not, extend PIP or explore role change per policy.

Step 8 – Document
• Store meeting notes, dates, metrics securely for compliance.

Outcome
• Jane gets tangible support and clear expectations.
• Project timeline protected; team morale maintained.

instruction: Can you implement a python tool that is intended to run black and isort when used?

performance_to_description.excellent:
• The answer contains a COMPLETE, RUNNABLE Python program (or clearly-marked module + entry-point script) that a grader can copy into a file, run with `python <file>.py --help`, and immediately use.
• Both black AND isort are executed – in that order (isort first, then black).  The grader should be able to see two distinct calls such as `subprocess.call(["isort", …])` followed by `subprocess.call(["black", …])`, or two API calls.
• The program accepts **one or more positional paths** (files or directories).  A grader can type exactly the example shown, e.g. `reformat src tests` or `python reformat.py src tests`, and see the tools process those paths.
• A "check-only" mode is present under a conventional flag (`--check`, `-c`, or `--diff`) that LEAVES FILES UNCHANGED but returns a non-zero exit status (commonly 1) if formatting would be required.
• Exit codes match industry conventions: 0 = everything already formatted, 1 = reformatting needed (non-fatal), 2+ = fatal error (missing dependency, invalid path, etc.).  The exact numbers may differ but **they must be documented and distinguish success / needs-changes / error**.
• Works on *multiple* paths and nested directories (no hard-coded single file assumptions).
• If either dependency is missing, the program prints a clear one-line instruction such as `pip install black isort` **and exits non-zero instead of showing a stack-trace**.
• The grader can deliberately give a non-existent path like `reformat does_not_exist.py` and receive a clean, user-friendly error message.
Example lines the grader should see in the code (not necessarily verbatim):
```
_run(["isort", *paths, "--check-only" if check else "--atomic"])  # isort first
_run(["black", *paths, "--check" if check else "--fast"])        # black second
```
performance_to_description.good:
• Code is runnable and both tools are executed, **but one critical detail is missing or slightly wrong**.  Typical issues that still earn “good”:  
  – black is run before isort.  
  – `--check` mode exists but exit status is always 0.  
  – The script only accepts **one** path even though it is positional.  
• Dependencies are not checked explicitly, but a standard `ImportError` stack-trace is the only failure.
• Minor edge-cases (e.g., nested directories) might break, **but the happy path works**.
performance_to_description.fair:
• Only ONE of the required tools is actually executed (e.g., runs black but forgets isort) **OR** the code is obviously incomplete (pseudocode placeholders, missing imports) but *could* be finished with small effort.
• CLI accepts paths in a hard-coded way (e.g., expects exactly `.`), so graders cannot supply arbitrary directories.
• No check/dry-run mode.
• Exit code is always 0 regardless of outcome.
• Error handling is minimal; missing dependencies raise raw stack-traces.
performance_to_description.poor:
• No runnable code at all (just English description), **OR** code that cannot even be parsed by Python (SyntaxError).
• Does not invoke black nor isort, or only describes what would happen.
• Ignores assignment requirements entirely.

performance_to_description.excellent:
• Uses argparse / click / typer with a `--help` screen that lists: description, positional *paths*, a `--check/-c` flag, and exit codes (0/1/2).  Crowd-workers can run `python tool.py --help` and **see** this information.
• The answer itself provides **copy-paste-ready examples**, e.g.:
  `reformat src tests`  (format in place)
  `reformat -c .`       (CI check)
• Option names follow black/isort conventions (`--check`, not `--dry`).
• If the answer shows packaging info (e.g., `pyproject.toml` with `[project.scripts] reformat = "reformat:main"`) or explains `pip install -e .`, graders mark this criterion as excellent.
• No OS-specific assumptions (works on Windows and Unix; avoids hard-coded `python3.11`).
performance_to_description.good:
• Uses argparse (or equivalent) so `--help` exists, **but** some information is missing (no exit-code explanation, poor examples, or non-standard flag names).
• Packaging/installation instructions are absent OR partially incorrect, but the script can still be run with `python file.py …`.
• Minor platform assumptions (e.g., mentions `python3` only) that wouldn’t block most users.
performance_to_description.fair:
• CLI is a manual `sys.argv` parse (no `--help`), or the help text is extremely sparse.
• Flags differ from community conventions (e.g., `--dryrun` instead of `--check`) causing potential confusion.
• No usage examples; evaluator must guess how to run the script.
performance_to_description.poor:
• No command-line interface: user must edit constants in the file or the tool is purely theoretical.
• No instructions at all; even an experienced user cannot tell how to invoke it.

performance_to_description.excellent:
• Script proactively tests for the presence of `black` and `isort` with `shutil.which()` or `importlib` and exits with a FRIENDLY message (`Required dependency 'black' is not installed …`).
• Invalid paths (non-existent file or directory without permission) produce a clear, single-line error and non-zero exit status **without a stack-trace**.
• Distinguishes **needs-changes (exit-code 1)** from **fatal error (exit-code 2)** so CI jobs can act accordingly.
• Captures and propagates non-zero exits from black/isort (e.g., syntax error in file) without crashing.
• Code is modular (functions) so that unit tests *could* be added; some answers even include a tiny test.
performance_to_description.good:
• Basic try/except around subprocess calls catches most crashes, but the same exit-code is reused for all failures (e.g., always 1).
• Missing dependencies show a stack-trace but the rest of the program is sound.
• Invalid paths cause an unhandled exception, but common cases (tools failing) are handled.
performance_to_description.fair:
• A blanket `except Exception: pass` hides errors; program may silently succeed or always return 0 on failure.
• No dependency checks; ImportError is unhandled.
• Program crashes on trivial issues such as read-only files.
performance_to_description.poor: • No error handling at all: any problem (missing tool, bad path) produces a Python traceback and the tool exits with status 0 or no exit at all.

performance_to_description.excellent:
• Submitted code itself PASSSES `black` (max line length 88) and `isort` (imports alphabetised & grouped).  A grader can run `black --check <file>` and receive *no* diff.
• Functions are small, verb-named (`reformat`, `run_command`), each with a concise docstring explaining parameters and return values.
• Type hints are present (`def _run(cmd: List[str]) -> int:`) improving readability.
• Helper functions abstract repeated logic (building commands, dependency checks) instead of copy-pasting.
• Project layout is minimal but clean (e.g., `src/`, `tests/`, `pyproject.toml`).
performance_to_description.good:
• Code is mostly formatted (maybe one 120-character line slips through) and imports are in a reasonable order.
• Docstrings OR type hints are present, but not both.  Functions may be a bit long but still readable.
• Some duplication exists but is minor.
performance_to_description.fair:
• Code does not conform to black/isort.  Long lines and mixed import ordering are obvious.
• Few or no docstrings; variables like `x`, `y` instead of descriptive names.
• Monolithic 150-line `main()` function that mixes parsing, logic, and printing.
performance_to_description.poor:
• Hard-to-read spaghetti: global variables everywhere, no functions, no comments.
• Unformatted (tabs, inconsistent indentation) and clearly never run through black or isort.

performance_to_description.excellent:
• Narrative explanation (if any) is brief, on-topic, and free of generic AI filler.
• No factual mistakes (does NOT claim that black sorts imports, etc.).
• Variable / function names are descriptive; comments are present *only* where the intent is non-obvious.
• The entire response (code + text) fits on ≤ 250 lines — concise yet complete.
performance_to_description.good:
• One or two minor digressions or redundant sentences, but overall clear.
• Tiny factual slip that doesn’t affect functionality (e.g., states black’s default line length is 90 instead of 88).
performance_to_description.fair:
• Noticeable amount of fluff text; graders must sift through to find the code.
• Several factual errors but code still works.
performance_to_description.poor:
• Rambling, off-topic, or contains blatant misinformation about black/isort.
• Hard for graders to understand where the answer is or how to run it.

excellent_response:
#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""reformat.py – Run isort followed by black on the given paths.

$ reformat src/ tests/        # formats in-place
$ reformat -c src/ tests/     # check only, no changes written

Exit status:
    0 – all files already well-formatted
    1 – files would be reformatted or another non-fatal issue occurred
    2 – fatal error (e.g., missing dependency)
"""
from __future__ import annotations

import argparse
import shutil
import subprocess
import sys
from pathlib import Path
from typing import List

EXIT_OK = 0
EXIT_NEEDS_CHANGES = 1
EXIT_FATAL = 2


def _ensure_dep(binary: str) -> None:
    """Abort with clear message if *binary* is not importable / executable."""

    if shutil.which(binary):
        return  # callable via subprocess
    try:
        __import__(binary)
    except ImportError:  # pragma: no cover
        print(
            f"Required dependency '{binary}' is not installed.\n"
            f"Run:    python -m pip install {binary}",
            file=sys.stderr,
        )
        sys.exit(EXIT_FATAL)


def _run(cmd: List[str]) -> int:
    """Run *cmd* and return its exit status, echoing output live."""

    print("$", " ".join(cmd))
    return subprocess.call(cmd)


def reformat(paths: List[str], check: bool = False) -> int:
    """Run isort *then* black on *paths*. Return combined exit code."""

    isort_cmd = ["isort", *paths, "--check-only" if check else "--atomic"]
    black_cmd = ["black", *paths, "--check" if check else "--fast"]

    rc_isort = _run(isort_cmd)
    rc_black = _run(black_cmd)

    return EXIT_OK if (rc_isort == rc_black == 0) else EXIT_NEEDS_CHANGES


def main() -> None:  # pragma: no cover
    parser = argparse.ArgumentParser(
        prog="reformat",
        description="Run isort followed by black on the supplied files/directories.",
    )
    parser.add_argument(
        "paths",
        nargs="+",
        help="One or more files or directories. Use '.' for the current directory.",
    )
    parser.add_argument(
        "-c",
        "--check",
        action="store_true",
        help="Do not modify files; just return a non-zero status if formatting is needed.",
    )

    args = parser.parse_args()

    _ensure_dep("black")
    _ensure_dep("isort")

    sys.exit(reformat(args.paths, check=args.check))


if __name__ == "__main__":  # pragma: no cover
    main()

# pyproject.toml excerpt so the script can be installed
#----------------------------------------------
#[project]
#name = "reformatter"
#version = "0.1.0"
#requires-python = ">=3.8"
#dependencies = [
#    "black>=23.7.0",
#    "isort>=5.12.0",
#]
#
#[project.scripts]
#reformat = "reformat:main"
#----------------------------------------------

# Usage examples
# --------------
# Format everything under src and tests
#     reformat src tests
#
# Check in CI (no changes allowed)
#     reformat -c . || { echo "❌ Code is not formatted."; exit 1; }

instruction:
Struggling with procrastination, I seek effective methods to start my day for maintaining productivity. Please provide 5 specific, actionable methods. Present these in a Markdown table format with the following columns: 'Method Number', 'Method Description', and 'Expected Outcome'. Each description should be concise, limited to one or two sentences. Here's an example of how the table should look:

Method Number	Method Description	Expected Outcome
1	[Example method]	[Example outcome]
Please fill in this table with real methods and outcomes."

performance_to_description.excellent:
• Response consists of one and only one Git-Hub style Markdown table using pipe (|) characters. 
• The header row is exactly the three phrases: "Method Number", "Method Description", "Expected Outcome" (capitalization variations like Title Case are acceptable, wording must match). 
• A separator row of --- (or :---) exists directly beneath the header. 
• Exactly five body rows are present, numbered 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 in the first column, with no blanks or duplicates. 
• No extra paragraphs, bullet lists, greetings, or code-block fences appear before or after the table. 
• All cells render (each data line begins and ends with | and has 2 internal | characters); no broken lines. 
• Every description cell is 1–2 sentences and ≤35 words. 
Example of an excellent first two rows:
| Method Number | Method Description | Expected Outcome |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | Apply the Two-Minute Rule: immediately finish any task that takes ≤2 min. | Generates quick momentum and clears small tasks. |
performance_to_description.good: Meets the table requirement but has 1 minor deviation that does not hinder understanding, e.g., a short explanatory sentence after the table, header written "Method #" instead of "Method Number", or one description containing 3 short sentences. No more than one such issue.
performance_to_description.fair: Multiple specification problems: 4 or 6 rows instead of 5, header labels partially wrong (e.g., "Outcome"), inclusion of an intro paragraph, or descriptions regularly exceeding 2 sentences. Table is still recognisable and readable.
performance_to_description.poor: Not presented as a valid Markdown table OR severe errors such as missing header row, mixed bullet list/table, un-numbered methods, or substantial stray text that violates the prompt.

performance_to_description.excellent:
• Each of the 5 methods describes a concrete, immediately doable morning action (e.g., "launch a 25-minute Pomodoro before checking email").
• Details such as time frames, tools, or steps are included so the user could try it tomorrow with no research.
• Methods are distinct—no two rows repeat the same core technique.
• None require expensive equipment, long-term training, or expert supervision.
Example excellent method: "Spend 5 minutes listing today’s Top-3 tasks in a notebook immediately after coffee."
performance_to_description.good: Most (4/5) methods are specific and actionable; one method is somewhat vague (e.g., "organise your workspace") or overlaps slightly with another suggestion, but overall implementable.
performance_to_description.fair: Only 2–3 methods give clear, immediate actions; several are generic ("be mindful"), need outside research ("learn GTD methodology"), or significantly overlap each other.
performance_to_description.poor: Methods are largely abstract, non-actionable ("try harder"), or impossible to enact immediately ("complete a 30-day habit challenge"). Little to no guidance on what to do.

performance_to_description.excellent:
• The set draws from strategies commonly cited in productivity literature or behavioral science (e.g., Two-Minute Rule, Pomodoro, Implementation Intentions, mindfulness).
• Each method directly targets a known procrastination driver such as decision fatigue, distraction, or lack of structure.
• No pseudoscientific or medically dubious claims (e.g., crystal therapy) appear.
• Suggestions span cognitive, behavioral, and environmental angles, showing variety.
Example of strong evidence link: "Mindful breathing reduces rumination, which studies associate with task avoidance."
performance_to_description.good: Most methods are relevant and plausible; one suggestion might have limited evidence (e.g., cold shower) but is still generally accepted, and no clearly false claims are present.
performance_to_description.fair: Several methods have weak or unclear ties to procrastination, or at least one relies on questionable evidence (e.g., proprietary supplement). No outright harmful advice is given.
performance_to_description.poor: Advice is predominantly irrelevant or pseudoscientific (e.g., "sun-gaze for 15 minutes to rewire your brain") or fails to address procrastination at all.

performance_to_description.excellent:
• Every outcome is a short, specific, and plausible benefit linked to reduced procrastination or increased morning productivity (e.g., "reduces decision fatigue").

Below is an answer that would score “Excellent” on every rubric dimension.

——————————
Five Non-Rotational Methods to Generate Electricity (meeting all constraints)

1. Photovoltaic (Solar Cells)
   • Principle: The photovoltaic effect—photons strike a p-n junction in a semiconductor (e.g., crystalline silicon, CdTe, GaAs), liberating charge carriers that are separated by the internal electric field to produce direct current (DC).
   • Real-world example: A standard 60-cell silicon rooftop panel (~1.7 m²) outputs ≈300 W under full noon sunlight.

2. Hydrogen–Oxygen Fuel Cell
   • Principle: Electrochemical conversion. At the anode 2 H₂ → 4 H⁺ + 4 e⁻; at the cathode O₂ + 4 H⁺ + 4 e⁻ → 2 H₂O. Electrons travel through the external circuit providing power with no moving parts.
   • Real-world example: The Proton-Exchange-Membrane (PEM) stack in the 2023 Toyota Mirai delivers up to 128 kW of electrical power.

3. Thermoelectric Generator (Seebeck Effect)
   • Principle: A temperature difference across junctions of Bi₂Te₃ and Sb₂Te₃ causes charge carriers to diffuse from hot to cold, generating a voltage (~200 µV K⁻¹ per junction).
   • Real-world example: Voyager 1’s radioisotope Thermoelectric Generator uses a 500 °C–100 °C gradient to supply ≈140 W for onboard instruments (still solid-state—no turbine).

4. Piezoelectric Energy Harvesting
   • Principle: Crystals like lead-zirconate-titanate (PZT) develop an electric field when mechanically compressed or stretched. Ambient vibrations or footsteps create alternating voltage that can be rectified.
   • Real-world example: Piezoelectric floor tiles installed at Shibuya Station in Tokyo generate ~5 mW per step, sufficient to power nearby LED signage.

5. Triboelectric Nano-Generator (TENG)
   • Principle: Contact electrification & electrostatic induction. Two materials with different triboelectric affinities (e.g., PTFE and aluminum) repeatedly contact and separate (sliding or tapping), transferring electrons and inducing a current through attached electrodes.
   • Real-world example: Wearable TENG patches demonstrated by Zhong Lin Wang’s group at Georgia Tech harvest arm-swing motion to run a 1.2 V wristwatch LCD.

All five methods avoid hydro, steam, geothermal, nuclear, biomass, wind, tidal sources, and use NO turbines or rotating coils.

Position Paper: A Consortium-Driven Innovation Testbed for Critical Mineral Recovery from Mining Waste
-------------------------------------------------------------
Executive Summary
The global energy transition is accelerating demand for lithium, cobalt, nickel, rare-earth elements (REEs), vanadium and other critical minerals by 400–600 % before 2035 (IEA Critical Minerals Review, 2023). At the same time, 100+ Gt of legacy tailings worldwide lock away an estimated US$1 trn of unrecovered metals (McKinsey, 2022) while generating >10 Gt CO₂-eq of lifecycle emissions. We propose establishing a "Critical Minerals Innovation Testbed" (CMIT) — a consortium of mining companies, equipment vendors, universities, and national labs — to pilot and de-risk advanced extraction and waste-valorisation technologies. By turning liabilities into assets, members can meet ESG targets, unlock new revenue streams, and strengthen supply security while sharing cost and IP risk. This paper summarises the feasibility, outlines the testbed architecture, and invites industry partners to contribute feedstock, pilot sites, capital, and expertise toward a multi-million-dollar proposal to the U.S. DOE (INFRA-E-23-014), Canada’s Critical Minerals R&D Program, and the Grantham & Sloan Foundations.

1. Strategic Context
• Supply Risk: 83 % of REE separation capacity is in China (USGS, 2022); Russia controls 17 % of global nickel Class 1 supply.
• Regulatory Tailwind: U.S. Inflation Reduction Act (2022) offers 10 % Advanced Manufacturing Production Credit for domestically refined critical minerals; EU Critical Raw Materials Act (2023) sets a 25 % recycling target by 2030.
• Untapped Resource: Historic tailings at Bingham Canyon (Utah) contain 0.04 % Sc and up to 150 ppm REE; Olympic Dam (Australia) tailings host >100 kt uranium and 60 kt cobalt equivalents.

2. Feasibility of Extracting Critical Minerals from Mining Waste
Technical Feasibility
• Heterogeneity: Modern hyperspectral mapping (e.g., ESA Sentinel-2) plus on-site XRF scanning allows 10 m resolution grade modelling of legacy dumps.
• Proven Processes: Rio Tinto’s Kennecott pilot recovered 20 t/y tellurium from copper electrolyte sludge in 2021; Vale’s Thompson tailings reprocessing yields 1,600 t/y nickel via bio-oxidation.
• Metallurgical Pathways: Sequential leaching (glycine→ionic liquid) achieves 92 % REE recovery from Bayan Obo tailings at pH 4, 60 °C (Li et al., 2022).
Economic Feasibility
• CAPEX < US$25 M for a 50 kt/y modular plant using High-Pressure Grinding Rolls (HPGR) + sulfite bioleach; IRR > 22 % at NdPr oxide price of $90/kg.
• By-product Credits: Selling inert geopolymer bricks made from treated tailings can offset 10–15 % of OPEX.
Environmental & Social Feasibility
• Detoxification cuts acid drainage by 95 % (Net Acid Generating test) and lowers dust PM₂.₅ by 70 %.
• Conversion of 1 Mt waste into construction aggregate avoids ~800 kg CO₂ per tonne compared with Portland cement.

3. Critical Minerals Innovation Testbed — Core Technology Pillars
Pillar 1: Advanced Characterisation & Digital Twins
1. Drone-mounted LiDAR + hyperspectral imaging for volumetric & grade mapping.
2. AI/ML geometallurgy platform (Digital Twin) predicting recoveries and CO₂ footprint.

Pillar 2: Smart Comminution & Liberation
3. High-Pressure Grinding Rolls (HPGR) with real-time acoustic sensors.
4. Microwave-assisted selective comminution to pre-weaken silicate gangue.

Pillar 3: Precision Separation
5. X-ray transmission (XRT) & laser-induced breakdown spectroscopy (LIBS) sensor-based ore sorting.
6. Hydrocyclone-microfluidic hybrid separators for <20 µm particles.
7. Nanofiltration membranes targeting Sc and Ga.

Pillar 4: Novel Extraction Chemistry
8. Glycine-based heap leaching (low-toxicity, recyclable reagent).
9. Deep-eutectic solvents (DES) for Co-Ni selective extraction.
10. Bio-leaching consortia (Acidithiobacillus ferrooxidans & Sulfobacillus thermosulfidooxidans) operating at pH 1.6.
11. Supercritical CO₂ with organophosphorus extractants for REE strip.
12. Mechanochemical activation (planetary milling + Na₂CO₃) to unlock refractory phases.

Pillar 5: Metal Recovery & Refining
13. Membrane solvent extraction (MSX) for Nd/Pr split.
14. Electrowinning with pulse-reverse current to reduce Mn impurity.
15. Continuous ion-exchange (CIX) columns for Li from mica tailings.

Pillar 6: Waste-to-Value & Environmental Modules
16. Geopolymerisation of neutralised tailings into bricks.
17. Carbon-mineralisation of ultramafic waste (magnesium silicates) sequestering up to 0.6 t CO₂/t waste.
18. Passive in-situ biocovers to suppress acid mine drainage.

4. Consortium & Governance Model
• Members: Anchor miners (e.g., Freeport-McMoRan, Teck), OEMs (Metso, FLSmidth), academic partners (UT Austin, UBC), national labs (NREL, ORNL).
• Contributions: Tailings feedstock (>50 kt each), site access, in-kind equipment loans, cash (minimum US$2 M per founding member), data sharing.
• IP Policy: Results pre-competitive; foreground IP shared through royalty-free licence among contributors for 5 years, then open.
• Management: 11-seat board (5 industry, 3 academia, 2 government observers, 1 independent ESG advisor). Technical Advisory Committee oversees TRL progression.

5. Funding Strategy
• Government: DOE Advanced Processing for Critical Minerals (up to US$30 M, 20 % cost-share), NRCan Critical Minerals R&D (CA$15 M), ARPA-E MINER program.
• Foundations: Sloan (Circular Economy), Grantham (Climate Positive Materials).
• Milestone-based tranche release linked to KPIs: ≥85 % metal recovery, ≤0.5 kg SO₂/t processed, sequestration of ≥50 kg CO₂/t.

6. Roadmap & Next Steps
2024 Q3 – Secure LOIs from at least five mining partners; finalise testbed site shortlist (Utah, Ontario, Queensland).
2025 Q1 – Commission 5 t/h modular pilot plant; deliver Phase I data pack.
2026 Q4 – Scale to 50 t/h demonstration; publish peer-reviewed LCA; file patents on DES recycling loop.

Conclusion & Call to Action
Mining firms face dual imperatives: secure critical mineral supply and minimise environmental footprint. The CMIT offers a capital-efficient, low-risk pathway to achieve both. We invite interested companies to join the consortium by 30 June 2024 to co-author the DOE proposal and gain first-mover advantage in the US$150 bn circular-mineral economy.

Below is an end-to-end example that would score “Excellent” on all criteria.

Assume production code lives in my_module.py:

```python
# my_module.py
from io import BytesIO

def func2(buf: BytesIO):
    # Real implementation writes bytes to the buffer and returns None
    buf.write(b"real impl")


def func1():
    buf = BytesIO()
    func2(buf)  # We will mock this in tests
    return buf  # Could also do something else with buf in real code
```

Unit test (test_my_module.py):

```python
from io import BytesIO
from unittest.mock import patch
import my_module

def test_func1_calls_func2_and_writes_correct_bytes():
    """func1 should pass a BytesIO to func2, and func2 should write expected bytes."""
    expected_bytes = b"fake data"  # determine what the fake func2 will write

    # Replacement for func2 that mimics its side-effect only
    def fake_func2(buffer_passed: BytesIO):
        assert isinstance(buffer_passed, BytesIO)  # sanity check on signature
        buffer_passed.write(expected_bytes)        # side-effect identical to prod
        # No return (real func2 returns None)

    # Patch WHERE func1 looks up func2: my_module.func2
    with patch("my_module.func2", side_effect=fake_func2) as mock_func2:
        result_buf = my_module.func1()  # call the function under test

        # --- Assertions ---
        mock_func2.assert_called_once()

        # Grab the very same BytesIO instance func1 created
        sent_buf = mock_func2.call_args.args[0]
        sent_buf.seek(0)
        assert sent_buf.read() == expected_bytes

        # If func1 returns the buffer, the two should be identical
        result_buf.seek(0)
        assert result_buf.read() == expected_bytes

        sent_buf.close()  # optional cleanup; BytesIO is memory-only
```

Why this test is correct:
1. `patch("my_module.func2", …)` uses the exact dotted path that `func1` will dereference, so the real implementation is never executed.
2. `side_effect` lets us *run* our replacement (`fake_func2`) each time the mock is invoked; because the real func2 returns `None`, we don’t use `return_value`.
3. We verify **both** interaction (call count) and state (bytes written). Seeking to position 0 ensures a clean read.
4. The code imports only standard-library modules, so anyone with Python ≥3.8 can run it.
5. Clean, deterministic, and no hidden global state.

excellent_response:
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
A Practical Introduction to Monads in Haskell
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
1. The 20-Second Summary
A Monad is a design pattern in Haskell that allows you to chain computations that live inside a context (for example, “might fail”, “involves IO”, or “has many results”) while making that plumbing look like ordinary straight-line code.

2. Formal Definition
In Prelude (base ≥ 4.13):
```haskell
class Applicative m => Monad m where
  (>>=)  :: m a -> (a -> m b) -> m b  -- bind
  (>>)   :: m a -> m b -> m b          -- sequencing (discard first result)
  return :: a -> m a                   -- inject value into the context (deprecated: use pure)
```

3. The Three Monad Laws (Must Hold for Any Valid Instance)
  1. Left identity   :  return a >>= f    =  f a
  2. Right identity  :  m >>= return      =  m
  3. Associativity   : (m >>= f) >>= g    =  m >>= (\x -> f x >>= g)
Violating them causes surprising runtime behaviour—e.g., lost effects or duplicated IO.

4. Real-Life Analogies
• Maybe – “Fragile Package”
  Think of `Maybe` as a postal box that might arrive damaged (Nothing). Bind (>>=) opens the box only if it arrived intact; otherwise every further step is skipped.
• IO – “Recipe Card”
  An IO value is not the cake—it’s a step-by-step recipe. The runtime is the chef who eventually executes it. Chaining recipes with >>= forms a bigger recipe without running anything yet.
• List – “Choose-Your-Own Adventure”
  A list embodies many possible worlds. Bind tries every world in chapter 1 and continues each branch independently, returning all possible endings.

5. Concrete Code Examples
(a) Maybe: safe math that may fail
```haskell
safeDiv :: Double -> Double -> Maybe Double
safeDiv _ 0 = Nothing
safeDiv x y = Just (x / y)

demoMaybe :: Maybe Double
demoMaybe = do
  a <- safeDiv 10 2   -- Just 5
  safeDiv a 0         -- Nothing, rest short-circuits
```
`demoMaybe` evaluates to `Nothing`.

(b) IO: Echo two lines
```haskell
echoTwo :: IO ()
echoTwo = do
  l1 <- getLine
  l2 <- getLine
  putStrLn (l1 ++ l2)
```
`do`-notation is exactly sugared >>= :
```haskell
echoTwo = getLine >>= \l1 -> getLine >>= \l2 -> putStrLn (l1 ++ l2)
```

(c) List: Cartesian product
```haskell
pairs :: [(Int,Int)]
pairs = do
  x <- [1,2]
  y <- [3,4]
  return (x,y)   -- ⇒ [(1,3),(1,4),(2,3),(2,4)]
```

(d) Either: accumulating errors
```haskell
toInt :: String -> Either String Int
toInt s | all isDigit s = Right (read s)
        | otherwise     = Left  "Not a number"
```

6. Monad Myths Busted
• “return exits the function” – No. It just wraps a value.
• “IO magically performs effects” – No. The runtime performs effects when main :: IO () is evaluated.
• “All containers are monads and vice-versa” – Some monads aren’t containers (e.g., (->) r); some containers aren’t monads (e.g., Data.Set).

7. When to Reach for a Monad
  – Sequencing computations with context
  – Managing side-effects (IO)
  – Early exit on failure (Maybe, Either)
  – Non-determinism (List)

8. Further Reading
  • LYAHFGG – Ch. 12, 13
  • "Monad Transformers Step by Step" – M. P. Jones
  • Hutton & Meijer (1998) "Monads in Practice"

;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;
;; 0. Warm-up: A Reminder of Lists in Scheme
;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;
;; In Scheme, a program itself is written as parenthesised lists.
;; Example: The source code (+ 1 2) is literally the list: '(+ 1 2)

(define data '(+ 1 2))          ;; data is now a list with three elements
;; We can inspect it exactly like any other list:
(car data)  ;; => +
(cadr data) ;; => 1

;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;
;; 1. Code *as* Data: Quoting and Evaluating
;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;
;; The quote (') operator tells Scheme NOT to evaluate its argument.
;; The eval procedure does the opposite: evaluate a datum as code.

(eval data) ;; => 3  (we just turned data back into running code!)

;; Common pitfall: eval works in the *current* environment; avoid
;; using it on untrusted data, or you will have security issues.

;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;
;; 2. Generating Programs with list and quasiquote
;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;
;; Suppose we want a function that, given a number n, produces code that
;; adds n to any argument x. First we build the list structure:

(define (adder-code n)
  `(lambda (x) (+ x ,n)))   ;; quasiquote + unquote (comma)

(adder-code 7)  ;; => '(lambda (x) (+ x 7))

;; We can now turn the result into a procedure:
(define add-7 (eval (adder-code 7)))
(add-7 5) ;; => 12

;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;
;; 3. Stepping Up: Writing a Macro (compile-time program generation)
;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;
;; With macros, Scheme shifts program generation to compile time.
;; Here is a tiny "when" macro re-implemented using syntax-rules.

(define-syntax my-when
  (syntax-rules ()
    [(my-when condition body ...)
     (if condition (begin body ...))]))

;; Usage:
(my-when (> 3 2)
  (display "Yes!\n")
  (display "Done.\n"))
;; Expands to (if (> 3 2) (begin ...)) before runtime.

;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;
;; 4. Culmination: A Toy Interpreter Written in Scheme
;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;
;; Finally, because Scheme data == Scheme code, we can write a small
;; subset interpreter in ~25 lines. It recognises numbers, the symbol
;; '+, and simple application.

(define (tiny-eval expr)
  (cond [(number? expr) expr]
        [(and (pair? expr) (eq? (car expr) '+))
         (+ (tiny-eval (cadr expr)) (tiny-eval (caddr expr)))]
        [(pair? expr)
         (apply (tiny-eval (car expr))   ; evaluate operator
                (map tiny-eval (cdr expr)))]))

(tiny-eval '((lambda (x) (+ x 1)) 41)) ;; => 42

;; This interpreter treats its input purely as data, yet the data are
;; valid Scheme expressions – demonstrating "programs AS data".

;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;
;; 5. Key Take-aways
;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;
;;  • In Scheme, source code is literally list data (homoiconic).
;;  • quote prevents evaluation; eval forces it.
;;  • quasiquote/unquote make program construction ergonomic.
;;  • Macros move program generation to compile time, enhancing
;;    performance and safety.
;;  • Because of these features, we can write interpreters, DSLs, and
;;    domain-specific code generators concisely.

;; End of lecture.

Here is one straightforward way to make exactly $1.00 using exactly 19 U.S. coins:

Breakdown of coins
• 18 nickels (18 × 5¢)  = 90¢
•  1 dime      (1  × 10¢) = 10¢
----------------------------------
                             100¢ = $1.00

Verification
Coin count: 18 + 1 = 19 coins ✔️
Value check: 90¢ + 10¢ = 100¢ = $1.00 ✔️

How I found it (brief reasoning)
I needed 19 coins whose values sum to 100¢. Limiting myself to nickels (5¢) and dimes (10¢), I set up two equations:
   n + d = 19             (total coins)
   5n + 10d = 100     (total value in cents)
Substituting n = 19 – d into the second gives 5(19 – d) + 10d = 100 → 95 – 5d + 10d = 100 → 5d = 5 → d = 1, so n = 18.

Other valid combinations (not required but shown for variety):

• 5 pennies, 12 nickels, 1 dime, 1 quarter → 5 + 12 + 1 + 1 = 19 coins; 5¢ + 60¢ + 10¢ + 25¢ = 100¢.
Each example fully satisfies the assignment.

Price of 3 pears = 3 × 25¢ = 75¢
Price of 1 lemon = 10¢
Total spent = 75¢ + 10¢ = 85¢
Paid with $1.00 = 100¢
Change owed = 100¢ − 85¢ = 15¢

To receive an odd number of coins, we look for a grouping of U.S. coins whose total is 15¢ and whose count is odd. The simplest such grouping is:
• 5¢ + 5¢ + 5¢ = 15¢ → 3 coins (odd)
A dime (10¢) + a nickel (5¢) would be only 2 coins (even) and therefore does not satisfy the preference.

Therefore, you will get three 5-cent coins — three nickels — as your change.

-- 1. Meta table that registers every logical schema version
CREATE TABLE schema_version (
    version_no          INTEGER PRIMARY KEY,
    released_at         TIMESTAMP NOT NULL DEFAULT CURRENT_TIMESTAMP,
    released_by         VARCHAR(100) NOT NULL,
    notes               TEXT
);

--    Primary key of version tables is (anchor_id, version_no).
--    All FKs that reference a versioned entity must include BOTH columns so integrity is preserved per version.

---------------------------
-- Example entity: Product
---------------------------
CREATE TABLE product_anchor (
    product_id SERIAL PRIMARY KEY
);

CREATE TABLE product_v (
    product_id   INTEGER,
    version_no   INTEGER REFERENCES schema_version(version_no),
    sku          VARCHAR(50) NOT NULL,
    name         TEXT        NOT NULL,
    price_cents  INTEGER     NOT NULL CHECK(price_cents >= 0),
    valid_from   TIMESTAMP   NOT NULL DEFAULT CURRENT_TIMESTAMP,
    valid_to     TIMESTAMP,
    PRIMARY KEY (product_id, version_no),
    FOREIGN KEY (product_id) REFERENCES product_anchor(product_id)
);

---------------------------
-- Example entity: Order
---------------------------
CREATE TABLE order_anchor (
    order_id SERIAL PRIMARY KEY
);

CREATE TABLE order_v (
    order_id      INTEGER,
    version_no    INTEGER REFERENCES schema_version(version_no),
    customer_name VARCHAR(200) NOT NULL,
    order_date    DATE         NOT NULL,
    PRIMARY KEY (order_id, version_no),
    FOREIGN KEY (order_id) REFERENCES order_anchor(order_id)
);

-- Junction table that references a PARTICULAR product and order version
CREATE TABLE order_item_v (
    order_id    INTEGER,
    order_ver   INTEGER,
    product_id  INTEGER,
    product_ver INTEGER,
    qty         SMALLINT  NOT NULL CHECK(qty > 0),
    PRIMARY KEY (order_id, order_ver, product_id, product_ver),
    FOREIGN KEY (order_id, order_ver)
        REFERENCES order_v(order_id, version_no)
        ON DELETE CASCADE,
    FOREIGN KEY (product_id, product_ver)
        REFERENCES product_v(product_id, version_no)
        ON DELETE RESTRICT
);

-------------------------------------------------
-- Convenience views for “current” (latest) state
-------------------------------------------------
CREATE VIEW product_current AS
SELECT p.*
FROM   product_v p
JOIN   (SELECT product_id, MAX(version_no) AS latest_version
         FROM product_v GROUP BY product_id) x
  ON   x.product_id = p.product_id AND x.latest_version = p.version_no;

CREATE VIEW order_current AS
SELECT o.*
FROM   order_v o
JOIN   (SELECT order_id, MAX(version_no) AS latest_version
         FROM order_v GROUP BY order_id) x
  ON   x.order_id = o.order_id AND x.latest_version = o.version_no;

-------------------------------------------------
-- Example workflow: create schema version 2, raise price of product 3
-------------------------------------------------
INSERT INTO schema_version(version_no, released_by, notes)
VALUES (2, 'alice', 'raise price of product 3, add discount column to order_items');

INSERT INTO product_v(product_id, version_no, sku, name, price_cents)
SELECT product_id, 2, sku, name, price_cents * 1.10
FROM   product_v
WHERE  product_id = 3 AND version_no = 1;

-- Any new rows in order_item_v for version 2 MUST reference product version 2 and order version 2, enforced by FK.

-------------------------------------------------
-- Query historic order with correct product prices at that time
-------------------------------------------------
SELECT oi.qty, p.name, p.price_cents
FROM   order_item_v oi
JOIN   product_v   p  ON (p.product_id, p.version_no) = (oi.product_id, oi.product_ver)
WHERE  (oi.order_id, oi.order_ver) = (42, 1);

-------------------------------------------------
-- Discussion & Trade-offs
-------------------------------------------------
-- • Pros: Strong referential integrity across all versions; no deletes or updates needed in place (copy-on-write).
-- • Cons: Storage growth is linear with number of versions; composite keys make SQL verbose; ORM tools need customizing.
-- • Alternative: SQL:2011 system-versioned tables (supported by PostgreSQL 16, SQL Server 2016) which automate the history table.
-- • Indexing: composite PKs already index (id, version_no); add separate indexes on version_no for fast “current” filtering.
-- • Cascade strategy: restrict deletes on anchor tables; allow cascading deletes within a version.
-- • Migration: New columns added only to *_v tables; existing anchor tables remain stable, simplifying application code.
criteria: Complete and Correct Versioning Schema Design

excellent_response:
INFLAMED JOINT (ARTHRITIS)

1. Definition & Pathophysiology
• Arthritis = inflammation of the synovial membrane and peri-articular tissues; contrast: arthralgia is pain WITHOUT inflammation.
• Classical signs: rubor (redness), calor (warmth), tumor (swelling/effusion), dolor (pain, esp. on movement), and loss of function.
• Cytokine-driven synovitis (IL-1, TNF-α) ↑ vascular permeability → effusion; unchecked neutrophil enzymes lead to cartilage destruction.
• Synovial fluid: turbid; septic arthritis usually WBC >50 000/µL (>90 % neutrophils); gout shows needle-shaped monosodium urate crystals with strong negative birefringence.

2. Clinical Presentation
History
• ACUTE (<48 h) mono-arthritis = septic joint or crystal disease; subacute/chronic poly-arthritis suggests autoimmune cause.
• Morning stiffness >30 min, night pain, or constitutional symptoms (fever ≥38 °C, malaise, weight loss).
Examination
• Erythematous, warm, tense joint with visible effusion.
• Severe tenderness; active AND passive ROM markedly limited (e.g., knee flexion stopped at 20°).
• Positive bulge/ballottement test for knee; patient unable to bear full weight.

3. Emergency Referral (RED FLAGS – same-day orthopaedic/rheumatology review)
• Suspected SEPTIC ARTHRITIS: hot swollen joint PLUS any of – fever ≥38 °C, immunosuppression, prosthetic joint, recent injection.
• Rapidly progressive pain/swelling or inability to bear weight.
• Neurovascular compromise: pale foot, cap refill >4 s, absent dorsalis pedis pulse.
• Hemarthrosis in anticoagulated or haemophilia patients.
• Child <16 y with acute limp or suspected septic joint.
Rationale: irreversible cartilage damage & systemic sepsis can occur within 24 h – urgent arthrocentesis (within 1 h) and IV antibiotics are required.

4. Common Causes of Joint Inflammation
A. Infectious – Staphylococcus aureus (most common), Neisseria gonorrhoeae, Streptococcus spp., TB, Lyme (Borrelia burgdorferi), viral (parvovirus B19, hepatitis B/C).
B. Crystal-induced – Gout (monosodium urate, 1st MTP), Pseudogout (CPPD, knee/wrist).
C. Autoimmune/Inflammatory – Rheumatoid arthritis, psoriatic arthritis, systemic lupus erythematosus, ankylosing spondylitis, juvenile idiopathic arthritis.
D. Post-infectious/Reactive – Chlamydia, Campylobacter, Salmonella, Shigella.
E. Traumatic/Hemorrhagic – Hemarthrosis after ACL tear, in haemophilia, or on warfarin; osteoarthritis flare with secondary synovitis.

Prompt recognition and referral of red-flag presentations prevent permanent disability and sepsis.

instruction:
Write an ACL config for Tailscale that has three groups in it

nill
family
servers


Everything that is included in the nill group has access to all servers of all three groups on all ports, what is included in the family group has the ability only to use any servers from any groups as exit-nodes, but does not have access to any services on the network servers, the servers group has access to 22/tcp, 80/tcp, 443/tcp to all servers of all three groups, and on other ports and protocols has no access

performance_to_description.excellent:
• The policy implements EVERY requirement exactly.
  – There is ONE rule that gives "group:nill" unrestricted reach (e.g. {"src":["group:nill"],"dst":["*:*"]}).
  – "group:family" can reach (a) any exit-node device (e.g. "tag:exit-node:*") and (b) the public Internet through the autogroup ("autogroup:internet:*") but CANNOT reach other peers/ports; no other accept rules mention group:family.
  – "group:servers" can reach ANY peer, but ONLY ports 22, 80, and 443 (rule resembles {"src":["group:servers"],"dst":["*:(22,80,443)"]}).
  – No broader rule appears later that re-opens access (e.g. a generic "accept *:*" or an inadvertent duplicate that widens scope).
  – Deny-by-default behaviour is relied on (omitting an explicit deny after the accept rules is fine).
  Evaluators can test with 3 thought-experiments:
     1) Would host in group:family be able to SSH (22) to a server? → NO.
     2) Would host in group:servers reach port 3306 on another server? → NO.
     3) Would host in group:nill open port 5000 to laptop? → YES.

     – Author split the group:servers rule into three separate single-port rules (22, 80, 443) – still correct.
     – Author also placed an explicit final deny block ("action":"deny","src":["*"],"dst":["*:*" ] ) – harmless.

instruction:
My situation is this: I’m setting up a server running at home Ubuntu to run an email server and a few other online services. As we all know, for my email to work reliably and not get blocked I need to have an unchanging public IP address. Due to my circumstances I am not able to get a static IP address through my ISP or change ISPs at the moment.

The solution I have found is to buy a 4G SIM card with a static IP (from an ISP that offers that), which I can then use with a USB dongle. However this 4G connection costs me substantially per MB to use.

But. Mail is the only server that needs a static IP address. For everything else using my home network connection and updating my DNS records with DDNS would be fine. I have tested this setup previously for other services and it has worked.

So. I was wondering. Would it in theory be possible to: connect the server to two network interfaces at the same time and route traffic depending on destination port. I.e. all outgoing connections to ports 25, 465, 587, and possibly 993 should be sent through the 4G dongle interface (enx344b50000000) and all other connections sent over eth0. Similarly, the server should listen for incoming connections on the same ports on enx344b50000000 and listen on all other ports (if allowed by ufw) on eth0.

I would then need DNS records from mail.mydomain.tld —> <4g static public IP> and mydomain.tld —> <home public IP> (updated with DDNS, and NAT configured on my home router).

Computers on the internet would then be able to seamlessly connect to these two IP addresses, not “realising” that they are in fact the same machine, as long as requests to mail.mydomain.tld are always on the above mentioned ports.

Question: Is this possible? Could it be a robust solution that works the way I hope? Would someone be able to help me set it up?

I have come across a few different guides in my DuckDuckGo-ing, I understand it has to do with setting a mark in iptables and assigning them to a table using ip route. However I haven't managed to get it to work yet, and many of these guides are for VPNs and they all seem to be slightly different to each other. So I thought I would ask about my own specific use case

rubric.criterion: Technical Accuracy and Completeness of Networking Solution

• Gives concrete, syntactically correct commands such as:
  - `iptables -t mangle -A OUTPUT -p tcp -m multiport --dports 25,465,587,993 -j MARK --set-mark 0x1`
  - `ip rule add fwmark 0x1 table mailroute`
  - `echo "100 mailroute" >> /etc/iproute2/rt_tables`
  - `ip route add default via 203.0.113.9 dev enx344b50000000 table mailroute`
• Creates an additional routing table and explains how to make routes persistent (e.g., netplan YAML or systemd-networkd dispatcher).
• Considers both directions of traffic: marks outbound packets *and* adds a rule such as `ip rule add from 203.0.113.10 table mailroute` so replies stay on the 4 G link.
• Mentions and gives command to loosen reverse-path filtering (`net.ipv4.conf.all.rp_filter=2`) or equivalent to avoid asymmetric routing problems.
• Shows how to bind mail services (Postfix, Dovecot) to the 4 G static address or otherwise ensure correct source IP.
• Warns about ISP port-25 blocking and potential MTU problems on LTE.
• Uses consistent, realistic interface names (e.g., eth0, enx344b50000000) and documentation IPs (203.0.113.0/24, 192.168.1.0/24).
A response missing **none** of the above bullets is "Excellent".

Commands may contain 1 minor syntax error that an experienced user could correct.  Still uses correct interface/IP examples.
performance_to_description.fair: Mentions that “you can mark packets” or “use multiple routing tables” but provides *few or no* concrete commands; or gives obviously incomplete/partially wrong commands (e.g., misses MARK or ip rule).  Ignores reply-traffic symmetry.  No discussion of rp_filter, binding, or port blocking.  Technical gaps would likely prevent the solution from working on first try.
performance_to_description.poor: States the setup is impossible or recommends a completely different/incorrect mechanism (e.g., simply adding two default routes and trusting metrics).  Provides no usable commands or includes commands that would break networking.  Demonstrates misunderstanding of Linux routing concepts.

• Presents the procedure in a logical, numbered sequence from interface config → routing tables → firewall → mail application → testing.
• Specifies *file locations* so changes persist (e.g., “place Netplan YAML in /etc/netplan/90-4g.yaml”, “save iptables rules with /etc/iptables/rules.v4”).

• Provides at least one concrete test command for connectivity (e.g., `curl --interface 203.0.113.10 ifconfig.me` or `telnet gmail-smtp-in.l.google.com 25`).
